Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a distinct covariate-shift scenario known as semi-supervised covariate shift (SSCS), characterized by an initial imbalance in both feature and label distributions. In SSCS, unlabelled data gradually accumulate more difficult instances. To tackle this challenge, we propose an innovative method called self-paced learning for semi-supervised covariate shift adaptation. This approach combines self-paced learning for feature adaptation and semi-supervised learning for invariance, creating a domain-invariant model that excels in both performance and flexibility. Experimental evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over conventional approaches. Additionally, we shed light on the theoretical underpinnings of our method in a covariate shift analysis and a new semi-supervised learning loss function. These findings reveal the links between our method's performance and its underlying theoretical components. As a result, self-paced learning offers a universal solution to general instances and semi-supervised covariate shift adaptation, applicable across a wide range of tasks. Moreover, it possesses robust domain adaptation capabilities, extending beyond classification to inclusive tasks, such as dimensionality reduction, regression, and both supervised and unsupervised classification. Lastly, we showcase the applicability of our method in real-world tasks, including disease diagnosis and traffic prediction, highlighting its potential to tackle complex challenges in practical domains. Given its extensive generalizability, we refer to our method as the Deep Self-Paced Learning over Graphs (DSPLG) framework. Ultimately, our research contributes a comprehensive theoretical foundation and empirical evidence confirming the integration of adaptation and semi-supervised learning as a compelling strategy. This research has inspired a new generation of machine learning algorithms capable of tackling complex, real-world challenges. Given its extensive generality, we propose the concept of generalized adaptation, representing an emerging trend in covariate-shift adaptation. As evidenced by the empirical results, deep networks exhibit a natural inclination towards instance-weighting, contributing to the ongoing discussion on the effectiveness of shallow vs. deep learning methods in tackling covariate-shift adaptation. With covariate-shift adaptation representing an essential component of generalized adaptation, we posit that deep learning methods hold the potential to address complex, real-world challenges more effectively. As such, we believe that our research in this domain will inspire new generations of machine learning practitioners. Lastly, the empirical evidence suggests that instance-weighting constitutes a natural objective for deep networks, sparking an ongoing discussion

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. In particular, we propose the development of 'harmonics' neural networks that incorporate geometric structure into their design, demonstrating improved performance on standard computer vision benchmarks compared to conventional architectures such as ResNet, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. Importantly, the improved performance of the harmonics model is achieved without increasing its complexity or resource requirements for both quantized neural networks and general deep learning applications. Additionally, the geometric framework allows us to study the dynamics of deep learning architectures across multiple algorithmic layers, thereby gaining valuable insights into the functioning of the deep learning system as a whole. In particular, we observe that the improved performance of the harmonics model stems from its ability to reduce geometric structure in higher algorithmic layers, thereby mitigating the risk of overfitting and promoting smooth performance optimization across these layers. Importively, the geometric framework enables us to distinguish between different types of deep learning systems, including conventional networks, recurrent networks, and equilibrium propagations, based on their geometric structures rather than functional roles. As such, this geometric framework provides a much-needed theoretical framework for interpreting the experimental observations of deep learning performance, thereby facilitating guided algorithmic design of deep learning architectures at both module and algorithmic levels. In particular, we propose the development of a generative equilibrium propagation model that incorporates geometric structure into its design, demonstrating improved performance on standard image recognition benchmarks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, and promoting a more unified understanding of the deep learning system as a whole. Importantly, the geometric framework allows us to study the dynamics of the generative equilibrium propagation model across multiple algorithmic layers, thereby gaining valuable insights into its internal workings and promoting a more precise explanation for its improved performance. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the connections between the generative equilibrium propagation model and the variational autoencoder, thereby facilitating a more unified interpretation of the deep learning system as a whole and promoting a more accurate account

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm. Our research generalizes the findings of Cusagotto-Garcia-Stiller's work on fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})/\mathbb{Q}$ and partially addresses an open question posed by Cusagotto-Garcia-Stiller and Cui-Liu-Zeng's work on fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{d},\sqrt{1\pm\sqrt{3}})/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$. Furthermore, our work includes a computational aspect where we retrieve specific generator candidates based on field discriminants and their connection to a database containing discriminants of cubic fields up to a certain bound. Our results are particularly relevant since the found generators could potentially resolve an unresolved part of the generalization of the Weber-Dubreuil-Legendre conjecture for cubic fields as well as influence the conjecture's confirmed cases as stated in the stated paper. Additionally, our work examines the distribution of a particular quantity and discloses an interesting pattern that could shed light on the unsolved Fermat prime power conjecture. Our study also explores the behavior of a different diagnostic class number, which we prove to be infinite under a specific assumption, thus addressing an open question posed in a different paper. Lastly, our work includes explicit examples of our theoretical findings and sheds light on two specific problems. The first problem, initially introduced in a different paper, involves the behavior of a particular class number related to resolvent fields of quadratic extensions connected to cubic fields. The second problem, initially addressed in another paper, relates to the occurrence of a particular class number in fields resulting from the composition of two cubic fields. Our work also includes a revised version of a previously published result that describes the behavior of a particular class number

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online. This layer group database was designed to be flexible and adaptable to both theoretical and experimental applications, with potential uses including the visualization of symmetry operations and the identification of essential symmetry properties for phonons and electrons. A Python package called SYMPOL was developed to streamline the computation of these symmetry properties, making it compatible with the numerical data produced by tight-binding models. This layer group database and the associated computational tools enable SYMPOL to be an essential resource for building a comprehensive database of materials' electronic and phonon properties. This database can eventually support applications such as material design within the 2D materials category. This layer group database is now accessible online at www.pol-sym.org/layergroups, along with the detailed theoretical data for each of the 80 group sets, and the detailed method descriptions used to compute the symmetry properties. Additionally, the source code for the SYMPOL package can be found on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/pol-sym/pol-sym. This layer group database is continuously updated to ensure it remains up to date with any advancements in the relevant technology, and any new developments will be made publicly available at www.pol-sym.org. This is done to ensure that the data and method approach used to compute the symmetry properties can be freely accessed by the community. In the future, this database is planned to be expanded to include materials with hexagonal and trigonal symmetry patterns. This addition is anticipated to significantly boost the coverage of the theoretical data produced by SYMPOL. This potential expansion to include these symmetry patterns will not alter the existing structure of the database, as the category of 2D materials is distinct from the categories of materials with other symmetry patterns. This is made possible by the modular design of the theoretical data, which is organized within the POLSYm class module. This module is responsible for computing the symmetry properties of materials with layer or trigonal symmetry patterns, and is not involved in the computation of properties for materials with hexagonal symmetry patterns.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate to Bessel functions, thereby generalizing a previously discovered relationship. Additionally, the paper delves into the geometric connections between covariant derivatives of the momentum operators and the Riemannian vector bundle. This investigation leads to the discovery of an intriguing relationship between the Riemannian vector bundle and the curvature tensor. In particular, it is shown that for a connection associated with the momentum operators, the curvature tensor appears as the sum of two compatible connections, each curving in a specific direction. This result has implications for geometries with a compact structure and positive constant sectional curvature, such as S^3. In contrast, non-compact manifolds with a constant positive sectional curvature (such as hyperbolic space) lack this relationship between the Riemannian vector bundle and the curvature tensor. Ultimately, the paper concludes by examining the coupling of momentum operators on intrinsically curved manifolds, revealing novel relationships in this context. Specifically, it is shown that for any manifold with a Killing vector field, the coupling of momentum operators takes the form of a quadratic combination of the momentum operators themselves, thereby generalizing a previously discovered principle. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Detailed explanations are provided along with extensive numerical evidence that guarantees the stability of our approach. In an example simulation, we successfully apply this method to a challenging Lattice QCD problem with multiple fermion flavors. Our model has the advantage of adding very little overhead compared to conventional Monte Carlo methods and requires only a negligible adjustment to existing simulation protocols to tackle the sign problem. Our solution has the potential to accelerate future lattice QCD simulations by reducing them to the half-filling case, a pivotal breakthrough for the field. A related public code repository contains the implementation of our method for quick reference: https://github.com/indigo-lqcd/sign-problem-transport. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between top and bottom quark masses. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. Ultimately, we select two promising methods - fine-tuning with task-specific data and adapter tuning - and thoroughly evaluate their performance on zero-shot and few-shot tasks. Our findings reveal that adapter tuning yields superior results and requires significantly less computational resources compared to fine-tuning. Our selected methods lead to performance increases of 4.5 and 2.5 percentage points in German and Korean language models, respectively. Notably, adapter tuning demonstrates potential as a computationally efficient technique for expanding language models to new languages with minimal data requirements, making it suitable for scenarios with limited resources. Furthermore, they conducted high-resolution simulations tailored to the CB230 IRS1 system, incorporating a fast spinning core to replicate its distinctive characteristics. In low-mass binary formations, a binary system's mass was approximately $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$, but as the core's mass increased to $0.1 \, M_{\odot}$, a binary system's mass increased to around $0.05 \, M_{\odot}$. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. A collaborative human-AI pipeline is presented that uses a combination of machine and human intelligence to pinpoint the prevailing narratives, thereby outperforming existing large transformer models in a dataset-specific setting. Our findings reveal that large transformer models are susceptible to data-specific excellence, capable of detecting narrative extraction, text classification, and ranking, but faltering when presented with unseen domains. By means of thorough experiments, we highlight the efficacy of multi-task learning in enhancing model performance and uncover the distinct roles of machine and human intelligence in narrative detection. Lastly, we explore the practical implications of PAPYER on content understanding, fact verification, and discourse improvement, ultimately shedding light on the potential uses of social media content in informing societal discourse. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. This technique is modular and can be applied to existing adversarial training methods with minimal additional computational costs. The code for this project is freely accessible on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/fseitz/bnn-adversarial-training.

This study draws inspiration from multiple fields including the adversarial robustness community, who faced similar challenges in certifying models on perturbed data, and the BNN community, who struggled with the compromise between model uncertainty and accuracy. 

The core idea of this research is the integration of two key concepts: certification and uncertainty modeling. This fusion enabled the development of a novel loss function that balances both aspects, thereby allowing the certification of BNNs on various datasets with minimal computational costs. 

This study makes three key contributions to the machine learning community. Firstly, it proposes a novel combination of certification and uncertainty modeling through the integration of Bayesian learning and adversarial training. Secondly, it introduces a modular approach applicable to existing adversarial training methods. Lastly, it demonstrates the practical value of certification in BNNs, particularly in uncertainty-calibrated models. 

In conclusion, this research showcases the significance of certification in BNNs. The proposed approach achieves robustness to potential attacks while ensuring uncertainty calibration, thereby providing reliable outcomes in applications demanding the highest standards. This study paves the way for the deployment of BNNs in critical systems, such as autonomous driving and medical diagnosis systems.

To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor, and we observed a significant correlation between a rumor's influence and its positive content. In contrast, the impact of a rumor that contains negative content is generally negligible. To further mitigate the risk of online rumors, we recommend implementing a early warning system that incorporates machine learning and identifying and blocking critical information to restrict the propagation of a rumor. Additionally, targeting and blocking a rumor's key adopters could help contain its spread. Meanwhile, accurately verifying a rumor with sufficient influence could significantly reduce public anxiety during the emergency. Lastly, spreading a counter-narrative by leveraging critical information and attenuating a rumor's influence could help reclaim public opinion. Our study offers a theoretical framework for addressing the pressing issue of online rumors and can inspire further research. To further improve the precision of our prediction, we suggest incorporating sequential features, floating features, and feature aggregation techniques in future studies. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Research Institute, across various locations in New Mexico, USA. The analysis revealed that compression ratios significantly influenced classification accuracies, with some methods performing better than others across the various datasets. Moreover, a correlation between compression ratios and classification accuracies was observed, suggesting that highly accurate classifications can be achieved with relatively high compression ratios, thereby indicating the feasibility of effectively reducing the dimensionality of hyperspectral pixels for classification tasks. The reconstruction errors of the methods examined revealed that there is often disparity between compression ratio and pixel classification accuracy, thereby underscoring the need for further investigation of pixel classification techniques. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of more efficient hyperspectral image dimensionality reduction methods, particularly those utilizing deep learning approaches, and can potentially be extended to the realm of multispectral images as well. Moreover, the research is expected to benefit remote sensing applications, including but not limited to, object-oriented analysis and classification of hyperspectral images. The existing code can be accessed at https://github.com/RS-SIRI-NM/Hyperspectral_PixelDimensionality_Reduction. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making selection somewhat daunting. Despite this, few studies have systematically examined the effects of loss functions on the training of deep neural networks. In this research, we bridge this knowledge gap by investigating how various loss functions influence the learning trajectories and outcomes of deep neural networks. Our findings reveal that certain loss functions, even those initially considered marginal, can yield exceptional performance on benchmark datasets, underscoring the need for a customized loss function tailored to the inherent characteristics of the problem at hand. Moreover, we demonstrate that the development of such an optimal loss function is feasible within a relatively limited number of iterations. Our proposed method serves as a low-cost alternative to traditional regularization techniques and is adaptable to a range of iterative training methods, including stochastic gradient descent, momentum optimization, and evolutionary computing. Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy of our approach in enhancing the performance of the default loss function on challenging datasets and showcase its simplicity and broad applicability. Our research posits that loss function optimization is a viable means of enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of neural network training. Our proposed method also paves the way for a comprehensive loss function benchmark that evaluates the resilience of a loss function to adversarial perturbations, thereby supplementing traditional criteria like sparsity promotion, parameter reduction, and model constraints, and facilitating the selection of an appropriate loss function in the future. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. By applying the principles of conservation, such as energy and momentum, parquet theory is capable of producing structured expressions for life-like interactions that adhere to specific rules. The theory has been successfully employed in the modeling of electronic systems, particularly in doped Mott insulators, with notable applications including the description of high-temperature superconductors and magnetic plates. Although parquet theory is grounded in a perturbative framework, its applications extend beyond a linear perturbation, facilitated by its ability to describe the transfer of momenta from one element to another. The theory plays a pivotal role in understanding how the properties of individual elements within a system affect their collective behavior, with implications in the understanding of a system's response to external stimuli and its ability to undergo a phase transition. The generalization of parquet theory to the domain of quantum field theory, known as sagittarius theory, has enabled the description of systems with a hidden symmetry known as chiral invariance. The successful description of systems without a hidden symmetry, known as gondola theory, has paved the way for a theoretical model that can accurately describe the collective behaviors of a system at all scales, with a wide range of applications including the description of ferromagnetic plates, magnetic plates, and systems with topological quark properties. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in user behavior and dispatcher responses. By developing a data representation model, researchers created interactive safety dialogs and analyzed characteristics such as incidence rates, response times, and message length. Additionally, two studies were conducted: one examined the impact of dispatcher support on users, showing a 15% increase in response rates when dispatchers provided emotional support, and another explored the relationship between dialog structure and dispatcher work quality, classifying dispatchers' performance based on their conversation style. This research contributed to the development of various products, including a recommendation system that suggests suitable dispatchers for particular incidents, based on their previous conversations, and a dispatcher assignment model that matches dispatchers with incidents to optimize user response rates and enhance dialogue structure. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and randomly selected songs, we found that
most hit songs tend to be musically straightforward with characteristics close to
the average. This discovery aligns with the theory that songs with moderate levels of
variety tend to be most appealing. Furthermore, we observed patterns indicating
that hit songs generally do not lead the trend in musical diversity. Instead, the
popular songs often reflect the prevailing musical styles of the time in which they
were released. In contrast, randomly selected songs in different decades tend to
have different acoustic characteristics, reflecting the changing musical preferences
of the general public over time. Lastly, we explored the relationship between
melodic complexity and volume in the songs, revealing a notable decrease in
variety among hit songs since the 1960s. This means that today's hit songs tend to
be less musically diverse and simpler in melody compared to those of the same
category released several decades ago. In contrast, randomly selected songs show no
such decline. Overall, our analysis shows that the acoustic characteristics of
hit songs are distinct from those randomly selected songs. While randomly selected
songs exhibit changes in variety over time, hit songs tend to remain stable with
a lower level of diversity. In contrast, the volume of hit songs increased steadily
between the 1960s and 2000s. This variation in acoustic characteristics among
randomly selected songs may hold the key to understanding the public's preference for
these songs. In contrast, the distinct acoustic features of hit songs are likely the
result of selection bias. Furthermore, our results for the volume of hit songs may
be attributed to the increasing prevalence of electronic instruments. Lastly, the
rhythmic patterns in acoustic features of hit songs revealed an unexpected shift
in the preferred tempo of these songs, changing from slow to fast over the course
of several decades. This shift may be attributed to the influence of rock music. 
This analysis provides concrete evidence for this phenomenon. In contrast, the
rhythmic patterns in randomly selected songs show no such trend. Additionally, we
observed variety in song atmospheres using a new method and discovered a notable
increase in the volume of hit songs over the course of several decades

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. Meanwhile, we discovered that the double powerspace preserves core-compact properties in a uniform manner. Additionally, our analysis reveals an inconsistency in a previously published result claiming a direct relationship between core-compact properties of spaces and their Smyth powerspaces. Specifically, the proof provided in the referenced paper contains an error for locally compact spaces that are not compact. We also explored alternative representations of Smyth powerspaces using sheaves and locales to gain insights into their core-compact properties. Specifically, for a space with local compactness, we found a core-compact sheaf that represents its Smyth powerspace at the level of locales. Lastly, we discovered that the core-compact sheaf representation is not unique to spaces with local compactness, but rather any space with a core-compact sheaf presentation must have compactness as a necessary prerequisite. We also established that sheaf core-compact properties can be characterized through the continuous-lift monad, but this characterization fails for the Scott powerspace. Specifically, the Scott powerspace does not have core-compact properties, and as a consequence, it cannot be presented as a sheaf core-compact space. However, we found an alternative presentation of the Scott powerspace using upper sets that exhibit compactness as a necessary and sufficient prerequisite, and further revealed that the core-compact properties of upper sets present an axiomatizable framework for core-compact properties in spaces with local compactness. Moreover, we found that compactness acts as an axiomatizer for core-compact properties of spaces with local compactness. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated using the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimator and its modified versions. In this research, a new modified ATE estimator, referred to as the nAIPW ATE estimator, is introduced. The nAIPW ATE estimator is based on an initial insight that both the Average Integration Projection With Weighting (AIPW) ATE estimator and the traditional ATE estimator adhere to specific properties. The paper demonstrates that the nAIPW ATE estimator is consistent and provides asymptotic normal distribution results. Moreover, the research involves developing a variance estimator for the nAIPW ATE estimator. The computational efficiency of the proposed estimator is validated through simulations, which also highlight the advantages of the nAIPW ATE estimator over the AIPW ATE estimator in terms of efficiency and computational speed. The effectiveness of the proposed nAIPW ATE estimator is illustrated using comprehensive empirical analyses. The research codifies the developed estimators and corresponding simulation tools in an open-source R package named ATEestimators. The package is accessible on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ATEestimators/index.html. The package can be installed using command install.packages(ATEestimators), following instruction at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ATEestimators/readme.html. The package can be loaded using library(ATEestimators), with available functions summarized in section Overview of Functions. The main function, nAIPWATEestimator, can be invoked using command nAIPWATEestimator(Y, T, Z, Q0), as detailed in section Overview of Functions. The input arguments are defined in section Variable Definitions. The function returns an object containing the nAIPW ATE estimator, bias-corrected nAIPW ATE estimator, weighted nAIPW ATE estimator, and bias-corrected weighted nAIPW ATE estimator. The SEs for the ATE can be obtained using function VarEstimator. The package also includes supplementary materials, available at https://github.com/ungarabog/ATEestimators. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which results in an approximately unbiased estimation vector, by analysing the distribution of parameter estimates and identifying a regularisation method. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimator outperforms existing alternatives. The benefits of using this new estimator are showcased through applications in two real-world scenarios: modelling flood extremes and estimating the probability of a future record event. While developed using a Gaussian extreme value model, this estimator can be applied to other models of non-homogeneous Poisson processes. We include a supplementary material containing extensive numerical results and a code for implementing the estimator, developed using the R programming language. Several additional practical considerations are also discussed in the paper, such as the selection of prior distributions and how to specify the tuning parameter'm' in practice. The advantages of using this new estimator are highlighted through its application to modelling flood extremes and estimating the probability of a future record event. This research suggests various avenues for future research in this field. As an alternative to maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian analysis offers flexibility through the specification of prior distributions. We demonstrate this by investigating the impact of different prior distributions on the estimator and exploring the stability of the estimator when using the maximum likelihood estimates as priors. Furthermore, this paper proposes a method for specifying the tuning parameter'm' by analysing the distribution of parameter estimates and identifying a regularisation method. Numerical simulations demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed estimator compared to existing alternatives. The practical implications of using this new estimator are discussed, along with suggestions for future research. To apply this estimator in practical situations, one must specify a prior distribution for the parameters and select a suitable regularising'm' value. We outline the steps for achieving this, along with presenting the results of numerical simulations, which evaluate the performance of the proposed estimator in various scenarios. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our research introduces robust variants of four prominent offline RL techniques for tabular domains and analyzes their performance under the best-case and worst-case scenarios. Specifically, in the worst case, we establish a lower bound on the learning error and demonstrate that several robust algorithms achieve a nearly optimal rate of $O(\sqrt{d/K})$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of states or actions, $K$ denotes the number of training samples, and in the best case, we prove that some robust algorithms reach a nearly optimal rate of $O(\sqrt{\log(d)/K})$. Furthermore, we propose two new robust algorithms that surpass the worst-case bound, achieving a nearly optimal rate of $O(\sqrt{d/K})$ in a more realistic setting. Our empirical studies on adversarial RL in MuJoCo continuous domains back the theoretical findings, indicating a strong correlation between performance and the fraction of corrupted data. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both methods underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. The findings of this study can inform the development of methods for detecting out-of-distribution examples and guide research in this area in the future. Additionally, we released a dataset known as OOD Detectors called SROOD, comprising data with shifts that were not previously documented, along with an open-source Reproducibility Framework that facilitates research in this area, in the hope of promoting more accurate comparisons of detection methods. With this resource, researchers can conduct reproducible research in this area and develop new techniques for detecting out-of-distribution examples. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple other well-known convolutional problems. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. Our research highlights the importance of using detailed models to improve accuracy when estimating the magnitude of airborne transmission risks. Such models can inform the development of effective prevention strategies, including the optimization of ventilation systems, the placement of protective shields, and the control of passenger flow. Ultimately, these measures can help mitigate the spread of infectious diseases in various environments of all sizes. To facilitate the adoption of our model, we have created a user-friendly computer program that simulates the airflow and aerosol movement, allowing users to input parameters corresponding to specific setting and transportation methods, such as operating a bus with an urban ventilation system or using a portable inhalation device, in order to assess and visualize the resulting airborne transmission risks. This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. We conducted a comprehensive shell-model analysis of nuclear properties and compared our results to experimental findings. We then reported our computed $\beta$-decay attributes, such as the $\log ft$ values and the mean shape factors. This study marks the first theoretical calculation for $\log ft$ values in conjunction with these novel experimental data. Additionally, we also calculated the $\log ft$ results for $^{135}$Te ($7/2^-$) decaying into $^{135}$I with different $J$-values. These theoretical studies on $\beta$-decay properties provide valuable nuclear information that can aid in the interpretation of experimental data. Furthermore, these calculations have extended our understanding of nuclear properties, enabling us to make predictions about the half-lives of $^{139}$Te ($7/2^-$) and $^{141}$Te ($7/2^-$) decaying into $^{139}$I and $^{141}$I, respectively. These predictions are based on theoretical $\log ft$ results and are compared to half-life estimates derived from the model using $T_{1/2} = \log(0.693 \cdot \tau_\beta^{\rm exp}) - (\log ft + 0.40144)$. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program violations. Specifically, in our testing scenario, an exchange was using a double-sided auction module to automatically prevent violations when handling multiple quantity trade requests, ultimately preventing over-subscribed orders in our experiments. Overall, the verified code ran at a speed comparable to or just slightly slower than its unverified counterpart, indicating the practical utility of our research. Specifically, the verified code was on average 2.23 times slower in OCaml and 6.22 times slower in Haskell compared to the standard unverified code. Despite the potential slow execution speed of the verified code, the maximum delay in processing requests was under 10 milliseconds for our experiments, which is considered to be an acceptable level of performance for an exchange. As a result, our research shows that verified programming can be both practical and useful for developing reliable and efficient market logic modules. Specifically, the verified code can be freely obtained from the following location: https://git.iist.unl.pt/20077402/double-sided-auctions/-/tree/verilog. Additionally, all the market data used in our experiments can be accessed at the following location: https://git.iist.unl.pt/20077402/double-sided-auctions/-/tree/data. To ensure the accuracy of our research, the various branches in the git repository represent different stages of our development process: the'verilog' branch represents our initial verification of the classic double-sided auction algorithm using $\mathcal{VC}$P and OCaml, while the 'vcp' branch represents our verification of the classic double-sided auction algorithm using $\mathcal{VC}$P and Haskell. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach to modeling data-driven systems, one that can accommodate various levels of nonlinearity and hidden dynamics, while also being suitable for large-scale systems. Our method modifies a mass and matrix operator using sparse approximation with nonlinear constraints derived from observed data. This innovation enables the use of highly efficient numerical methods for solving partial differential equations and the application of dynamic mode decomposition to solve the resulting system, resulting in a data-driven model for large-scale systems with nonlinear interactions. We demonstrate our approach's accuracy and efficiency in multiple examples, including experimental data, where it provides precise predictions in short-term forecasting and high-resolution field reconstruction. We show that the existence of system constants can ensure the existence of solutions for this system, particularly lowering the regularity requirements for key variables, and obtain an estimate for the dissipation rate in terms of the initial conditions. Furthermore, we derive an $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}L^\infty$-estimate for a related system of transport equations, which has applications in nonlocal elasticity theory. These findings enhance and expand upon a previously published paper by Li and Zhou. We also include an appendix with supplementary results for a modified Averin-Bodor elasticity model. This model leads to a system of transport equations with unique properties and solutions that decay in time, and can be contrasted with a brittle material model. Additionally, we establish the local well-posedness of a related nonlocal parabolic system by obtaining $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}L^\infty$-estimates and specific bounds for the dissipation rate and solution growth. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a depth depth camera driver for Oculus VR systems, designing a depth-based sketch recognition framework, gathering and evaluating a benchmark dataset, and experimenting with air-drawn sketches versus written inputs in a VR setting. Our data analysis suggests that air-drawn sketches in a VR setting outperform written inputs. With a comprehensive dataset and study, we propose an alternative future direction, integrating sketch-based retrieval with online 3D model repositories to provide users with more flexible access to these resources. To facilitate reproducibility, we make our implementation, dataset, and sketch recognition framework publicly available. HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes, allowing them to refine the details of the planet's orbit. Data show that the time of the planet's closest approach to its star is now known to be 1.658648 ± 0.000185 days rather than 1.658731 ± 0.000090 days as previously thought. Additionally, the team's findings suggest that the planet's orbital path is not perfectly circular and may be slightly elliptical than previously assumed. These discoveries will ultimately aid in making precise measurements of the planet's atmosphere when it passes in front of its star. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Our SPQR decomposition approach enables more efficient parameterized solutions compared to forbidden-minor classification methods. We've also introduced new notions of SPQR trees, upward planar spanning trees, and upward geodesic trees, for which we've established effective algorithmic results. Our work contributes to the field of parameterized algorithms and provides insightful abstractions of certain parameterized subtree kernels. Our findings can be found in a new paper. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent information, including the fraction of the environment explored. A transformer-based attention mechanism is used to determine the useful content of this memory.
A graph neural network incorporates the fraction of the explored area along with past navigation experiences to build the long-term memory.
Experimental results on a new dataset show MemoNav outperforms state-of-the-art models, including a prevailing approach in the field, by significant margins. Moreover, MemoNav's architecture is presented as a modular structure, allowing for the integration of various memory components to facilitate flexible navigation. A related API allows for the creation of diverse navigation tasks, providing a useful resource for the community. The project's code can be found at: https://github.com/yangyangyang Yang/MemoNav. The dataset is available at: https://doi.org/10.2202/2416-8388.v7.2020-32.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in real-world conditions. This paper summarizes my past, present, and planned research into small cell optimization. Moving forward, I will concentrate on a newly utilized unlicensed band, the 6 GHz frequency, where emerging Wi-Fi and 5G NR technologies are likely to coexist. This new band offers considerable advantages for optimizing the infrastructure necessary to support emerging applications with demanding requirements. Furthermore, the increasing presence of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is expected to significantly impact future wireless infrastructure and utilization. This new challenge and opportunity will receive attention in my future research by focusing on optimizing the infrastructure utilizing the 6 GHz frequency to minimize the overhead created by UAV traffic. This will be achieved through the efficient management of air transport systems and the optimization of ground infrastructure utilizing ground-based radios to direct low-overhead aerial transport of customer premises equipment. This vision is part of a larger holistic transport system where ground and aerial infrastructure coordinate as a single entity to minimize overhead while maximizing customer premises data rates. This will result in a potentially groundbreaking transport system that could soon become the norm. This future vision will be developed into a viable model for optimization by leveraging the concepts of transport complexity and data rate requirements. Two key research questions will guide my future research: 1) how the 6 GHz frequency can be utilized efficiently with minimal overhead to connect customers through aerial transport, and 2) how ground infrastructure can be optimized using directional antennas to direct traffic to and from UAVs while promoting fair coexistence with other technologies. To address these challenges, several research tasks are planned including the development of an optimal transport model that minimizes overhead and meets the requirements of all connected customers, followed by the identification of efficient solutions using mathematical concepts and the implementation of this model using computational tools. Finally, my research will conclude with the simulation of optimal solutions by using real-world data and computing tools to establish benchmarks for practical applications. This research will contribute to the development of innovative transport systems that minimize overhead while maximizing data rates, and promote the utilization of the 6 GHz frequency

We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By adopting this symmetry perspective, we may uncover underlying principles governing operator growth and entanglement behaviors, thereby enhancing our understanding of these quantum system characteristics. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, allows for a better understanding of the highly-clustered nuclear structure. The study utilizes the TigRAS beamline at the ISOLDE-CERN, utilizing high-resolution total kinetic energy spectra of the three $\alpha$ particles resulting from the free-space decay of the Hoyle state. The analysis shows that the direct decay ratio of the Hoyle state, as an $\alpha$-condensate, is approximately 0.187 % of the total decay paths, resulting in a ratio of about 0.65 to the decay path through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state. The study indicates that the localized and weakly-bound $\alpha$ clusters in the Hoyle state play a significant role in its formation and that the non-resonant decay component is negligible. Furthermore, the study shows that the decay mechanism of the Hoyle state is different from that of the low-lying 0$^{+}$ states in $^{16}\mathrm{O}$. The study's results provide valuable information and insights about the clustered nuclear structure, paving the way for future research in this field. The ISOLDE-CERN experiment is the first to quantify the direct decay ratio of the Hoyle state at the 7.65 MeV level in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, resulting in a significant advancement in our understanding of the highly-clustered nuclear structure of the Hoyle state. The study's results are crucial and can be used to interpret the theoretical calculations of the clustered nuclear structure of the Hoyle state in the future. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type transition from quasi-static to dynamic behavior when the crack speed equals the shear wave speed; (iii) It's minimally affected by changes in fracture energy by adjusting the dissipation strength. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is a universal feature of fracture in 2D, while numerical challenges remain to extend this understanding to 3D. The following is a brief overview of our research approach. First, we developed a computational method that combines fracture and fluid dynamics using an explicit variational consistent formulation. Then, we applied the model to study the oscillatory instability in both linear and nonlinear elastic materials. The approach involved solving 2D explicit time-dependent partial differential equations that combine balance laws with dissipation terms. These equations extended the traditional governing equations for elastic solids by incorporating conservation laws of momentum, energy, and angular momentum, along with evolution equations for the crack and dissipation variables. By utilizing upwind numerical schemes, we solved the explicit time-dependent PDEs using an implicit time-stepping method. The approach resulted in a numerical method that combines fracture and fluid dynamics, observable in the form of a YouTube video. The video shows the oscillatory instability in a material with nonlinear elastic behavior near the crack, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of the intrinsic scales. The following is a brief description of the research outcomes. The explicit time-stepping method was successful in solving the given problem. The approach was found to be consistent with the governing equations of solid mechanics. The solutions were observed to be stable and convergent. The observed oscillatory instability in a material with nonlinear elastic behavior near the crack is consistent with the predicted theoretical results. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from an enhanced pairing contribution stemming from the Zeeman field-induced mixing of bands. Our analysis also indicates that the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as evidenced by the Zeeman field-induced half magnetic quantum flux production. These findings present an innovative model for realizing topologically non-Abelian states in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional settings, paving the way for the generation of fault-tolerant quantum computations. Furthermore, we proposed the possibility of observing spin transfer phenomena in scanning tunneling spectroscopy. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and accurately extract data from them. This study introduces two essential tasks: Identifying Factual Claims in Tabular Data and Retabling - both of which are critical to truly interpreting tables. Unlike existing methods that only consider linear table structures, we also account for non-linear tables. Unlike language-based approaches, we'll utilize the knowledge graph format for representing tables, allowing us to leverage existing graph technologies. This study presents innovative solutions for both tasks, along with two proposed models that utilize the knowledge graph format to evaluate the accuracy of our approaches. Experiment results demonstrate that our proposed Retabling model surpasses existing methods. Additionally, we've established a new dataset, comprising 1,112 questions based on 438 real-world tables, making it the first dataset of its kind. This dataset is available for download at https://github.com/ju-st/interpreting-tables. For our proposed project, the code can be accessed at https://github.com/aimeread/interpreting-tables. This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. Additionally, we consider some alternative theories based on real numbers and outline potential directions for further investigation. Lastly, we offer some reflective comments on the prevalent reliance of Quantum mechanics on complex formalism. This discussion aims to initiate dialogue on the fundamental nature of complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. 

In this article, we will specifically explore the following claims:

1. Quantum mechanics cannot be formulated solely using real numbers.
2. There is no inherent need to employ complex numbers in Quantum mechanics; rather, they arise naturally from the fundamental principles of the theory.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. When the graph is a circle graph, which is a graph where the nodes are connected based on the distance between them, we found a formula for beta_k for every k and graph size. Additionally, we found that the worst case time complexity of computing beta_k for every k and graph size is solvable in polynomial time. This makes circle graphs the first known class of graphs where the computation of beta_k is solvable in polynomial time, and we suspect this may also be true of other graphs where the nodes are connected based on the distance between each other in a line, such as those in the same class as the numbers 1 to 7 modulo a number. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. These reviews led me to the conclusion that the most efficient numerical methods for solving the flow equation are those that rely on simplifying assumptions and solving the resulting ordinary differential equation analytically. Conversely, solving the flow equation directly using numerical methods such as the finite difference method isn't advisable. Lastly, I've included a brief comparison of the approximations for the flow rate with depth, such as the flow rate approximated by Fourier Series and the Harlan Brown Approximation. This review aims to make the approximations more accessible to those working with the method of characteristics. 

This document was initially created in 2018 as part of my work on integrating numerical methods for solving the flow equation far away from the water table. It's now an online document where anyone can view the math supporting the method of characteristics. 

It's worth noting that the document is meant to be a reference guide rather than an instructional document. Potential readers who lack a background in mathematics may struggle to comprehend the documentation. 

In contrast, documents by Harlan Brown and others, such as Hantush-Mabey, are more suitable for less experienced mathematicians and hydrologists. 

Lastly, I'd like to extend a gratitude to Professor Hantush for inspiring this document, which is based on his work, and to the National Speleological Society for supporting this project through a grant.

Additionally, EAPrunedDTW was successfully integrated into time series forecasting and similarity evaluation tasks, demonstrating its capabilities in these domains. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially resulting in poor performance in other areas. We aim to improve student learning through targeted testing concepts by enabling instructors to provide more nuanced feedback using three novel feedback approaches based on inquiry-based learning principles. We demonstrate the efficacy of these feedback strategies, which we implemented using two testing tools for Python and Java, through feedback sessions with 29 undergraduate students and a professional tester. We observed improvements in test effectiveness, covering 94% of coverage metrics, while also providing more accurate coverage insights that minimize guesswork and promote structured testing methods with clear progress indicators. We retain the ability to easily modify and iterate on these feedback approaches based on emerging research findings. We plan to maintain this feedback infrastructure as a resource for the testing community. Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it. Moreover, this research proposes a novel framework to assess the degree of over-smoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks. Using this framework, the effects of over-smoothing on both node classification and graph representation can be evaluated. Empirical evidence demonstrates that the proposed measures effectively mitigate over-smoothing. The supporting code is available at https://github.com/GUoT-GCN/GUoT. 

In this research, the term 'over-smoothing' refers to the reduction in the variance of the activation function when applying successive layers of graph convolution, making it challenging for the network to learn meaningful features. The study also uses the term'smoothing factor' to describe the average decrease in the variance of the activation function across the nodes of a graph for a given graph convolutional layer. A graph convolutional layer is considered smooth if its smoothing factor is less than or equal to 0.5; otherwise, it is considered non-smooth. The upper bound of this quantity is referred to as the Smoothing Factor Upper Bound (SSUB). 

The SSUB has been formulated as the minimum eigenvalue of the transition probability matrix multiplied by the kernel size of the graph convolutional layer. For approximated graphs, it can be estimated using the inverse of the degree matrix times the logarithm of the kernel size. The upper bound for approximated graphs is more conservative than that for intrinsic graphs. 

The study has found that the Smoothing Factor Risk (SFR) increases with the number of graph convolutional layers, making the last layer potentially non-smoothing and explaining the phenomenon of over-smoothing. The SFR has also been found to decrease with the precision of the graph convolutional layer, making the approximate graph convolutional layer less susceptible to over-smoothing.
