Dark matter particle research has been conducted using a dataset of Z boson candidates accompanied by a significant amount of undetected energy produced by proton-proton collisions. Data was collected between 2016 and 2018 at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV using the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, equating to 137 fb^-1 of accumulated luminosity. By examining two distinct particle decays – one involving electron pairs and the other muon pairs – researchers have found no evidence to support the standard model's predictions. Based on this, scientists set new limits on the interaction of dark matter with other particles, including different types of mediator particles, as well as a hypothetical particle in a specific two-Higgs-doublet model. Researchers have also derived constraints for the cross-sectional probabilities associated with dark matter interacting through spin-dependent and spin-independent processes. Furthermore, a statistical analysis using resolved Z boson candidates has provided the tightest constraints to date on dark matter interacting via a general vector mediator. These findings represent the most stringent restrictions on dark matter models to date, exceeding the limits set by the International Linear Collider studies as well as the mono-X search for dark matter. In addition, a comprehensive list is given of the theoretical models affected by the newly established limits on dark matter. Lastly, a brief overview is provided of the technical specifications and performance characteristics of the CMS detector used in these studies. Specifically, analysis of data from the single LHC run failed to yield evidence for dark matter. Thus, future studies at higher luminosity runs at the LHC might be able to detect dark matter. In a related development, final reports on the 2016 search for dark matter candidates involved in the decay of the Higgs boson produced in association with a bottom quark. Data used in this study came from the various methods employed by the CMS experiment to detect dark matter. In particular, one of these methods relied heavily on the decay of the Higgs boson produced in association with a bottom quark to establish the mass of the dark matter candidate. In this particular method, the mass of the dark matter candidate was found to be approximately 125 GeV. Conversely, another method used the distinct characteristics of the edge of the jet in hadron showers to establish the mass of the dark matter candidate. In this particular method, the mass of the dark matter candidate was found to be higher than 200 GeV. In yet another method used the distinct radiation patterns of electrons and muons to establish the mass of the dark matter candidate.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from Boer-Mulders, Drell-Yan, and Sivers functions. These functions are also connected to the alignment of quark spin vectors within transverse momentum and are related to the double spin asymmetry of the Drell-Yan process and the alignment of quark spin vectors within jets. Furthermore, we offer an example of a potential contribution to the alignment of quark spin vectors within jets related to the Boer-Mulders function. This contribution can be quantified through numerical calculations using parton distribution functions. Additionally, we suggest a relevant experimental investigation involving semi-inclusive jet production and identify both JLab9/KRISS and eIC colliders as suitable facilities for this research. However, we note that our proposed investigation is hampered by a lack of comprehensive data on Boer-Mulders function and quark spin alignment in final state jets. Consequently, we emphasize the need for more detailed theoretical calculations to further understand this phenomenon. Lastly, we outline potential future research topics centered around the alignment of quark spin vectors and their impact on jet production. These topics include double Drell-Yan process, differential Boer-Mulders function, and quark spin alignment in exclusive and semi-exclusive jet production, as well as an integrals of Boer-Mulders function and quark spin alignment in exclusive and semi-exclusive jet production. These topics provide a rich ground for theoretical exploration and can serve as a basis for analyzing potential future electron-ion colliders.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, and it gets closer to the truth as the available data become more reliable. A test then helps us determine whether the matrix of average relationships is essentially constant. A method for evaluating how well the available data fit the model, and comparing this to how well other models fit the data as well, is also provided. It can in fact tell us whether the models are different even if some of their assumptions about the data are similar. Two studies are presented to show how this approach works in practice. In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity directly relate to the horizontal measured foliations derived from the uniformization maps associated with its components that extend towards infinity. For a given hyperbolic surface that a pair of measured foliations, denoted by $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$, completely fill, our analysis reveals that when sufficiently small, multiplying both $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$ by a factor of $t>0$ results in unique representations as the foliations measured at infinity for a corresponding quasi-Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold. This new manifold is essentially an extended version of the given surface that approaches an infinite real number. Our finding is similar to another known theorem which asserts that a quasi-Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold can be constructed by gluing two hyperbolic surfaces together at their boundaries, a process known as hyperbolic surgery. Our method of fusion is distinct from hyperbolic surgery in that the measured foliations of the resulting three-dimensional manifold are directly obtained from the measured foliations of the surfaces being glued together. This direct relationship allows us to propose that hyperbolic surgery is a specific instance of a broader class of construction methods known as measured foliation surgery, which involves using measured foliations to determine the structure of the three-dimensional manifolds they fill. Measured foliation surgery can be thought of as an extension of the concept of Fenchel-Nielsen deformation, an important technique in the study of surfaces, to apply to three-dimensional manifolds. Our work also reveals an interesting connection between the maximum principle and the concept of compactification, as we demonstrate that the set of all hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds with a given measured foliation structure converging to a particular point serves as the compactified version of the manifold itself, thus offering a new approach to understanding the concept of compactification. Our method of proving this compactification is distinct from a previously known theorem which asserts that the set of all hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds with a given measured foliation structure converging to a particular point is compact and separately compact with respect to their convergence properties. Our approach is different in that we utilize the concept of half-pipe structures to understand the compactification of the manifold, a concept which allows us to calculate various properties such as Euler characteristics and the first Betti number. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  A database with real-world noise patterns is created and then used to develop a comparison of removal techniques for both types of distortions.  Results show that a combination of clarification techniques followed by feature extraction methods outperforms other approaches in accurately identifying heart conditions and detecting disease-related sounds.  A machine learning-based abnormality detection system that applies these methods achieves a high success rate of 90.9% and 91.7% on two different datasets, respectively.  To validate the reliability of the proposed solution, a detailed analysis of the results and the design of an end-to-end device for cardiac consultation were presented.  Significantly, a professional cardiologist's accuracy in diagnosing heart conditions from audio recordings increased by 7.7% after using the proposed method.  A software implementation of the proposed solution is available at \url{https://www.ida.fhg.de/4_103.html}.  A hardware implementation of the proposed solution can be installed at \url{https://www.ida.fhg.de/4_103.html}.  This study was funded by the European Social Fund (ESF). This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences. Our results suggest that auction designers may be able to boost revenue by creating credible auction environments. Additionally, our research highlights the potential for bid manipulation to be a concern in auctions that lack credibility. Ultimately, our study addresses a key gap in existing research by investigating the impact of auction integrity and provides insights into the complex relationship between auction theory and actual bidder behavior. Our results are particularly relevant to understanding the bid patterns seen in online platforms such as Google AdSense and Facebook auction bids. Given the growing trend of using auctions as a means of allocation and price determination, accurately comprehending bidder behavior, as identified in our study, could lead to significant financial gains. Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices, effectively reducing the problem for all Hessenberg functions. Secondly, for nonregular Hessenberg varieties, we identify a corresponding geometric vertex decomposition, comprising two distinct components: a nilpotent subsystem corresponding to the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety and a set of curvatures derived from the Fock-Goncharov coordinates. Lastly, as a consequence of our work, we demonstrate that the local defining ideal associated to any Hessenberg function is specified by a finitely generated module over the Weyl algebra A_{n-1}(ℂ), specifically with respect to the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety, thereby resolving an outstanding problem in the field. Furthermore, for the case of type A regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties, we assert that the set of indecomposable projectors modulo their 2-fold compositions encompasses the entire set of local defining ideals, providing a potentially groundbreaking decomposition that could influence the study of other varieties. In addition, the geometric vertex decomposition we introduced may serve as a basis for the development of an algebraic calculus, potentially facilitating the calculation of quantum K-theory for nilpotent symplectic resolutions, currently a major area of study in the field. In order to understand fast neutrino flavor conversion in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino flavor conversion occurs in regions close to the proto-neutron star where neutrino density is high and for certain energy levels, but this process is hindered by a lower energy threshold in regions further away from the star. Notably, this behavior differs from the typical density-contrast scenario commonly observed. Furthermore, our results indicate flavor conversion happens earlier and is more prevalent in larger regions surrounding the star, especially in explosions where neutrino escape rates are higher. This distinction could affect the distribution of electron and muon flavors following the initial explosion phase, potentially leading to an accumulation of electron antineutrinos due to a conversion process. This phenomenon could have significant implications for future experiments such as the DREAM/toe and KRAKEN projects, which aim to detect antineutrinos originating from supernovae events. The fast flavor conversion process may significantly impact the survival probability of antineutrinos, thereby influencing their detectable quantity. Consequently, this new mechanism could either enhance or diminish the sensitivity of these experiments in detecting supernovae events. Additionally, our research suggests that neutrino energy levels and matter asymmetry play a crucial part in flavor conversion occurring. Therefore, in the future, researchers should conduct various simulations involving distinct mass ranges and different explosions and non-explosions scenarios to thoroughly understand the phenomenon. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive an integrated outcome. Notably, the study found that using merely 15 crucial regions of interest for training yielded a 70.6% accuracy rate, surpassing the existing benchmark of 68.6% achieved with all regions. Furthermore, the researchers developed and tested novel models, namely Separate Channel CNN RNN with Attention, Separate Channel dilate CNN RNN with Attention, and Separate Channel CNN slicing RNN with Attention, to identify the most effective structure. The ASSRNN model emerged as the top performer, attaining a 70.46% accuracy rate with only 13 essential regions. The study's findings demonstrate that concentrating on the critical brain regions for ADHD diagnosis via deep learning can yield superior outcomes compared to using the entire brain. Additionally, the proposed models displayed higher performance than prior competition winners. The research hopes to provide insights for both researchers and clinicians to better understand the computational models' output in clinical settings. The code is available at https://github.com/ashishk211/DeepLearningBasedADHD. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases and are commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the website provides source code for reproduction and modification at http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000/src.html. In addition, we invite researchers to contribute to a growing data set comprising 1,581 newly created acronyms at https://github.com/QALM-Oregon/acronym-corpus. Lastly, our project is partially funded by a grant from the National Science Foundation. (DRL-1939792).

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. In this study, we demonstrate that quantum interference can also be a decisive factor in the thermal transport of charge through mesoscopic systems. The research involves a double quantum dot system coupled to an electron reservoir, where one dot is held at a fixed potential and the other can be electrically gated. The researchers observed how the interaction between dot states affects the flow of charge and heat under varying gate voltages. The key finding reveals that heat flow can be blocked while allowing a continuous charge current, a phenomenon that can be controlled through electrical means. The discovery provides a new avenue for the study of quantum interference in mesoscopic heat-trapping devices. The concept also lends itself to the exploration of more advanced thermal rectification mechanisms. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. We've further introduced special indexing symbols that enable the straightforward detection of differences between original and updated data objects, as well as the simultaneous updating of multiple objects at various locations within a segment with a single sequence output. A practical example demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed DNA-storage system in real-world scenarios. Comprehensive experimental studies were performed to evaluate the proposed DNA-storage system's capabilities, including sequence validation, the comparison of various sequencing strategies, the assessment of the impact of error, the impact of DNA degradation, the utilization of multiple storage segments, the realization of flexible and efficient low-level data storage operations, and the implementation of a high-level data storage interface. Additionally, we conducted the first thorough investigation into the overall sequence utilization ratio as the error rate decreases, and developed the fastest known sequence comparison algorithm suitable for DNA-data-storage applications. Our experimental results successfully validated key components of the proposed DNA-storage system, including the efficient reuse of PCR amplifiers, the efficient low-level data storage operation, and the efficient comparison of sequence comparison algorithms. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These results hold provided the entropy is bounded away from zero by a quantity linked to $\eta > 0$, and a no-go result indicates the non-existence of polynomial query algorithms for distributions with very low entropy. The analysis considers the most general input model - the quantum purified query access model - enabling handling of both classical distributions and quantum states. The study also establishes a lower bound on query complexity at $\Omega(n^{\frac{1}{3\gamma^2}})$ for approximating Shannon and von Neumann entropies multiplicatively. Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this study develops an innovative framework that divides the day into numerous short periods, enabling the calculation of average traffic demand, estimation of the probability of each, and consequent variation in flow measurements. Employing a non-parametric approach, the probability distribution of each period's traffic demand can be computed and used to simulate the probability of each period's traffic flow. Simulation results indicate that the probability of traffic flow at nodes and links differs significantly from the average traffic flow, especially during periods of high traffic volume. This study also proposes an efficient method for optimizing road network revenue by pairing each period's traffic flow with a corresponding probability estimate, thus maximizing the revenue based on a linear programming approach. Validation and case studies demonstrate the efficacy and practical applications of this proposed method. Ultimately, the research suggests that the proposed framework can serve as an effective tool for various transportation planning activities, such as planning and managing traffic information services, planning and managing traffic mitigation measures, and conducting in-depth analyses of the reliability of transportation networks. In particular, this study demonstrates that an additional 10% of the total number of periods can increase the accuracy of probability assessment and flow coupling, thus suggesting that transportation planners can utilize this proposed framework to make strategic decisions in the planning and management of transportation systems. In depth case studies indicate that an additional 10% of the total number of periods can enhance the reliability of traffic information, widen the options for traffic information services, and optimize traffic mitigation measures by incorporating probability estimates. In specific, this study examines three practical decision-making scenarios: planning traffic information services, managing traffic mitigation measures, and analyzing and planning transportation networks. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is observed in structured patterns for small lattices, whereas in larger lattices, it gives way to chaotic behavior. We demonstrate that this phase transition can be attributed to a well-known phenomenon in disordered systems called the "mott transition" typically seen in tightly bound electrons. Our research reveals that global phase coherence emerges through a sudden reorganization of the oscillations in the lattices, resulting in a significant decrease in the entropy of the system at the critical point. We also analyze the complexity of the patterns formed by the oscillations and their geometric characteristics, such as the distribution of energy across the lattice. Our detailed study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics in conserved systems with non-linear interactions. Furthermore, our findings have implications for advanced condensate systems, such as cold atom and electron systems. We explore the possibility of observing this phase transition experimentally using coupled nonlinear Josephson junctions. Our research marks the beginning of a new line of investigation into the phenomenon of global phase coherence in conserved systems and their geometric characteristics. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence, the paper shows that these algorithms generate uniform spanning trees with the same probability distribution, and this realization enables a faster hybrid method that leverages Wilson's algorithm with an adapted, faster Broder algorithm for early tree generation. This hybrid approach cuts down on the average number of steps required to produce a spanning tree, offering improved efficiency with a time complexity of O*(ln n). The study also explores the potential for similar accelerations with other spanning tree algorithms. Alongside the theoretical analysis, the paper also provides accompanying code for these algorithms. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal data points. Comprising sheet-music images, lyrical text, and synthesized audio, the dataset is comprised of three modalities, each represented by advanced models. This paper outlines the development of our music dataset and showcases the process behind our data collection, as well as initial methods applied to cross-modal retrieval tasks using MusicTM-Dataset. The proposed dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/dddzeng/MusicTM-Dataset. Our code is also available for reference. Additionally, the dataset has been recognized with an Honorable Mention award at the 2022 Workshop on Multimedia Analytics for Assistive Living at ACM Multimedia 2022. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and a defocusing cubic nonlinearity, dark solitons display the same characteristics as in the pure cubic defocusing model. However, adding variable refractive index significantly changes how we assess stability in the dark solitons. Notably, only isolated imaginary axis eigenvalues are found, and energy-based stability is applicable with exponentially weighted Sobolev spaces. Moreover, adding small external influences and confinement still yields spectrally stable solitons in the minimum points. The system's solitons persist as small waves travel through it, and we take this behavior into account when investigating the overall stability of dark solitons. The stability of solitons in a completely isolated segment of the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and cubic defocusing and focusing capabilities is also explored, and we demonstrate the ability to create stable, localized waves in this system, analogous to bright and dark solitons in the cubic defocusing model, by manipulating the system's parameters. The presence of variable refractive index allows for the creation of stable solitons with greater power in the focusing regime and stable solitons with greater power in the defocusing regime, and we observe an unusual feature where two solitons with the same characteristics can either attract or repel each other based on their relative power. Furthermore, we successfully identified the minimum power required for stable solitons in the system, and demonstrated the ability to transform stable solitons into localized waves with phase shifts. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume, and that optimally balanced designs require a multifaceted approach. By examining a variety of design examples, we provide insight into the various tradeoffs involved and how they might be navigated to achieve a specific design goal. Our work culminates in a comprehensive code framework, known as balmar, which is specifically tailored to address modular stellarator design challenges and can be applied in a variety of rotational stellarator design scenarios. Our design results are further supplemented by a detailed documentary explanation of the code framework and its usage, as well as a set of supplementary tools that enable the repetition of our design process for alternative coil set examples. Our research contributes to the growing field of stellarator design by providing a systematic methodology for achieving versatile designs with distinct rotational transform ranges, a range of design examples showcasing the applicability of our approach to diverse rotational stellarator design targets, and a freely available code framework that empowers the creative interpretation of our findings. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability. However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems is extremely challenging. We overcome this problem by using a novel algorithm that combines single-photon detection data with a model describing heat propagation. We test and validate the approach using two different experimental setups: one using a small reactor for catalytic hydrogen generation and the other using a microreactor for methane conversion. The results show that the algorithm can accurately determine temperature distributions in both cases, with errors below 1% when using a model-based approach and over 90% of data points matching experimental values better than a 2% error rate. Since our method doesn't need constant monitoring or supplementary measurements, it significantly reduces the need for experimental resources in fixed bed reactors analysis. Additionally, we observed the influence of particle size and flow rates on temperature distribution, which has practical applications for optimizing industrial processes. Due to its versatility, our technique can likely be applied to analyzing temperature patterns in various heat transfer systems. The algorithm's code is available for public use at https://github.com/Single-photon-metry/SPTE.Mice simulation code can also be found at https://github.com/Single-photon-metry/SPTE-Simulations. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments that play a crucial role in regulating various cellular functions. In this study, a theoretical model is employed to examine the effect of molecular interactions on the formation of droplets. The model incorporates two key components - nucleic acids and proteins - that undergo phase separation in the presence of a third component, a cellular fluid that exhibits phase incompatibility with the droplet liquid. The model also accounts for the movement of droplets within the cell and their tendency to merge with other droplets. The results show that droplet formation can occur at both small and large scales, with the size of droplets determined by an equilibrium between their volume and surface area. The model also predicts that droplets undergo cycles of rapid growth and shrinkage, driven by fluctuations in the concentration of proteins and nucleic acids in the cellular fluid. The theoretical framework developed in this study can be applied to experimental observations, providing insights into the behavior of droplets and their role in regulating cellular processes. The findings of this research have significant implications for our understanding of droplet-related phenomena in both artificial and natural systems. Ultimately, the model suggests that droplets can be utilized as a robust and efficient tool for regulating cellular processes, including the storage of genetic information and the regulation of protein expression. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Additionally, by reversing the causality of this b-principle, we arrive at a novel decomposition of the mapping class group of a surface with bounded geometry, characterized by its stable locus and a specific topological information set known as $K$. This relationship is represented by an algorithmic construction, which we refer to as the Morita-Miller machine. A significant consequence of this decomposition is the proof of an altered version of the Mumford Conjecture, which asserts the vanishing of the $b$-boundary class of the mapping class group of a surface with bounded geometry. Finally, by examining the reduced version of the Morita-Miller machine, we achieve a simplified characterization of the $K$-class, yielding a new interpretation of the classical Dehn's algorithm. Furthermore, through quantitative studies, an estimate of the average complexity of an arbitrary Dehn's algorithm, along with an assessment of an average version of the Slides Conjecture, can also be derived. Lastly, by exploring a variant of the Morita-Miller machine, we obtain a characterization of the $K$-class in surfaces with distinct geometric structures, leading to a simplified characterization of the $K$-class in surfaces with limited $k$-points, and also establish an average version of the Slides Conjecture for surfaces with limited $k$-points. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: the influence of the solver strategy for individual subdomains, the effect of differing subdomain solvers on performance, the impact of coarse solver choices, and the effect of varying overlap on performance. An AMD and Intel Core processor system is used for this comparison. Interestingly, the research reveals that BDDC can outperform AMG when the latter's coarse solver is an iterative linear solver, albeit at the expense of increased memory usage. Conversely, AMG emerges as the more efficient option when the successive over-relaxation algorithm is employed as the coarse solver. A potential explanation for these observations involves the differences in memory usage between the two preconditioners. Moreover, the research shows that both BDDC and AMG methods are capable of solving the system to the desired precision only after a relatively small number of iterations, irrespective of the subdomain solver used. A corresponding code for replicating this research is included in the supplementary materials. Based on these findings, the use of BDDC or AMG may be deemed suitable alternatives for solving cardiac mechanics problems. Ultimately, the choice of solver should be based on a careful evaluation of the trade-offs involving memory usage, computational speed, and programming complexity. This research provides valuable insights into the performance of different solvers in high-performance computing applications, including varying subdomain solvers and overlap regions in the BDDC algorithm. As such, it offers a useful resource for practitioners working in the field of computational mechanics. Additionally, this research can serve as a model for conducting similar performance evaluations on different high-performance computing solvers. As the need for scalable and efficient solution methods continues to grow with the rising nonlinearity in the model, the importance of comparative assessments of solution strategies will become increasingly pertinent. This research therefore contributes to the ongoing efforts to refine and adapt algebraic and algebraic solvers for practical use in the solution of various mechanical and material modeling challenges. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics. This paper presents a consolidated view of existing studies on tag system analysis, extracting key insights from this literature to guide future research on supported content collaboration. By extracting underlying themes from the literature and developing a taxonomy along with representative examples, this work positions itself as a gateway to this body of research, from which several avenues for further exploration are identified. Ultimately, the paper seeks to promote methodological diversity and encourage researchers to leverage existing knowledge in the field, while also highlighting promising areas for exploration in the hope of inspiring new studies. Experimental case studies are presented to demonstrate the practical value of tag system analysis in informing system design, including the development of TagCrowd, which won the first place prize at the ACM 2020 Web Science Cup. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. Moreover, we observed an enhancement of 5.4 dB in the transmission coefficient compared to a static microacoustic metagrating at 2 MHz. This research overcomes challenges in acoustic wave manipulation at the MHz frequency and paves the way for the integration of acoustic metagratings in practical ultrasound imaging applications. Moreover, the developed framework can be applied in the design of various devices, such as flat acoustic lenses and sensors, with similar properties. Lastly, we found that energy loss due to thermoviscous effects can be substantial even in microacoustic metagratings and must be considered during the design of polymer-based microacoustic devices at the MHz frequency. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, such as carefully crafted evaluation metrics and benchmark problems. To address this need, we present a new Learning to Localize Objects task as part of the Continual Learning in Reinforcement Learning (CRL) benchmark. This task requires objects to be localized efficiently on synthetic 2D maps with constant topology but varying contents, and we compare the performance of four established reinforcement learning continual learning methods, including Progressive Size Incremental Neural Network, Progressive Variable Importance, Episodic Memory, and Reinforcement Learning, in a persistent learning environment with constantly introduced new objects. The study highlights the 'curiosity-driven learning' approach employed by Episodic Memory and Reinforcement Learning as a crucial factor in tackling problems with large continua, and through in-depth analysis, we identify key limitations of the other methods and suggest potential improvements. The CRL benchmark, experimental design, and accompanying code are publicly available. The benchmark provides open-source 2D map generators that change incrementally to simulate the diverse situations encountered in real-world applications, and the benchmark itself is designed to promote discussion on evaluation metrics in continual learning. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatial Relationship Proposal Editor (SRoPE), addresses this issue by dynamically managing proposal types based on their difficulty levels, thereby optimizing the labeling process and accelerating the convergence towards high accuracy. The SRoPE framework can be applied to various complex vision tasks beyond VRD. Thorough experiments on three public datasets reveal significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our framework achieves relative improvements of 3% to 9% on the synthetic dataset Synthetic Scenes, and 2% to 6% on the real-world datasets LinckZFV and NUS-VRD, in terms of mean average precision. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Our work offers a crucial link between quantum information theory and the principles of continuous quantum measurement, making the QCC a useful tool for evaluating the quantum aspect of weak measurement procedures. In addition, our study highlights the differences between the predictive and the QCC approaches to quantifying quantum correlation. Importantly, our results show that the predictive measure can include classical elements, whereas the QCC is purely quantum in nature, relying solely on quantum process theory. We believe that the QCC will serve as a valuable instrument for evaluating the quantum nature of multiple queries in order to determine their ultimate quantum origin. We also compare it to the notion of quantum information, as defined by N. Mermin, and demonstrate that the two concepts are not equivalent, with the quantum information being the least sensitive to the measurement process. Lastly, our study exhibits the irreversible nature of the transition from the quantum information to the QCC when the measurement strength increases. The research conducted in this article is relevant to ongoing discussions regarding the notion of quantum information and has potential applications in the field of quantum information processing. The results obtained can be extended for studying the quantum correlation present in continuous weak measurement procedures involving bosonic fields, as well as the Scully-Schwinger effect in optomechanical systems. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results, allowing us to integrate both error correction and resource optimization objectives in the ILP formulation as distinct weights. Our proposed model was tested using a Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGA, yielding an average error rate of 0.49% and requiring fewer LUTs than the best available approaches, including those using fixed-point arithmetic and single precision floating-point formats. Specifically, our model outperformed existing MCM solutions, achieving a 7% improvement in LUT efficiency, along with a 35% reduction in LUTs required to accomplish 16-bit MCMs within a specified error margin. Our proposed model also facilitates hardware design acceleration, typically taking less than 1 minute to complete, compared to hours or days using other methods. Furthermore, we integrated a two-phase hardware evaluation that included both FPGA and ASIC technologies to provide a trustworthy evaluation of our model's performance in real-world applications. Our proposed approach successfully demonstrated its practicality, as demonstrated by the experimental results of our 65-bit, 8-bit, and 130-bit MCM implementations, showing considerable improvements in hardware efficiency, error rate, and multiplierless MCM area, respectively. Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments. This finding underscores the need for further research into the role of massive black holes in astrophysics. As a related notion, some of these massive black holes may be part of a new class of stellar black holes, known as $\beta$-decays, which could further influence the astrophysical environment. The presence of these hypothetical particles could also impact the universe's neutrino spectrum, according to some models. Ultimately, confirmation of Hawking radiation or the radio background would require detailed analysis of unsolved anomalies in astrophysics and cosmology, potentially providing new insights into the universe. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability. An equivalent characterisation of diagonalisability is presented, showing that it imposes significant restrictions on the possible structures of the constraints. Significant examples of diagonalisable constraints include, but are not limited to, equality, inequality, equivalence, and comparative unary predicates. It is proven that all surviving cases with non-monotonically soluble values can be reduced to a general-valued Max Cut, while those with monotonically soluble values can be reduced to known results. An alternative approach using lp-relaxation using the Sherali-Adams LP for general-valued CSPs with any constraints is proven to yield a PTAS for any solvable class. Lastly, sufficient conditions for a class to be resistant to PTAS are given when the constraints are binary. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established by various studies in the past few years, leading to the emergence of efficient syntactic parsing techniques such as the generalized parser and unsupervised parser, both grounded in self-attention mechanics. Notably, unlike other models, like the Transformer, which relies on specific multi-head attention mechanisms, these novel parsers utilize linear projection matrices for query and key transformations to facilitate syntactical extraction. To bridge this gap, our research delves into the critical elements influencing the effective utilization of pre-trained models in unsupervised parsing, focusing on key factors: syntactic dimension, head approximation, and masking strategies. Through an extensive analysis, we demonstrate that these novel parsers surpass the generalized parser and demonstrate promising results in unsupervised parsing, achieving performance on par with the current state-of-the-art models on diverse datasets spanning multiple languages, including English, German, and Finnish. Furthermore, our findings reveal that there is an optimal range of syntactic dimensions for model effectiveness. Additionally, our research highlights the significant role of head approximation in enhancing parsing accuracy and suggests that alternative modeling approaches might yield better results. Last but not least, our study shows that various masking strategies do not notably impact the model's performance. Based on these insights, we developed FinPar, a fast and efficient unsupervised parser, grounded in the generalized parser, which demonstrates remarkable speed, especially when compared to the unsupervised parser, with both models achieving similar accuracy on the Finnish dataset. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research focuses on tackling the challenge of semantic segmentation within complex, city-based environments, incorporating high-resolution hyperspectral images for enhanced performance. By leveraging advanced hyperspectral segmentation techniques combined with conditional random fields for structured modeling, we are able to achieve this goal. A sub-pixel CNN is utilized for generating dense label maps from sparse annotation, and our experimental findings, revealed through the CaViAr hyperspectral dataset, demonstrate that such an approach yields superior results when compared to traditional pixel-wise training methods. Moreover, this work highlights the significant advantages of applying hyperspectral images for semantic segmentation, showcasing a considerable improvement over standard RGB images. Comprehensive performance evaluations, including segmentation comparison and error analysis, are also presented. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints for the differential rotation and the location of the rotation transition interface, account for uncertainties in the surface layer, and verified that the measured differential rotation is stable over a long period of time. Given the available data, we cannot rule out a purely radial rotation pattern or a pattern with slow core rotation; yet, the observed behavior of this giant star contradicts theoretical predictions for angular momentum conservation. Based on the location of the rotation transition interface, we proposed possible scenarios, including the influence of tidal interactions with a companion star that is currently unseen or possibly absent, on the star's evolution and internal dynamics. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that rely heavily on real-world interaction data, researchers incorporate explicit or implicit regularization techniques. Unlike existing approaches, this research proposes a novel session-based recommendation framework called Selfencoder (SE), which harnesses the power of self-supervised learning to tackle the data sparsity issue. Unlike prior methods, SE develops a more sophisticated model architecture that encodes both item embeddings and their interactions within session sequences. Crucially, SE enables the generation of high-quality representation for target items in each session by learning the underlying structural patterns in the data. Empirical evaluations across three diverse dataset benchmarks demonstrate that SE outperforms existing state-of-the-art session-based recommendation models, including CoarseMatch, ASTGN, ASTFN, GRN, self-supervised learning approaches like Multi-view Contrastive Learning, Palomino, and a generative model called Reconstuction. Notably, SE also surpasses various counterfactual baseline strategies on two smaller datasets, namely CoarseMatch-Encdec and Palomino. Furthermore, SE analyzes the effectiveness of various regularization techniques used in session-based recommendation systems. Additionally, SE conducts thorough examinations of SE's architecture, confirming its ability to tackle data sparsity problems in comprehensive detail. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. A notable example illustrates how these integrals solve Bethe Ansatz equations for the Heisenberg model, shedding light on the relationship between graph moduli and spectral properties of graph-related systems. Our integrals may also be seen as motivic integrals, an idea explored further in a companion document. Finally, we present evidence suggesting the graph moduli space has a mixed motivic Hodge decomposition. Additionally, and connected to this finding, is the presence of Riemann's differential Galois group $G_{\rm Riem}$ within the general linear group, a finding prompted by the observance of invariants from the 1-forms on graph moduli, a notion devised by Muller, and the detection of a novel symplectic structure on graph double covers, as well as new identities linking Fourier transforms and the exponential function. Last, but not least, we present a novel algorithmic approach to solving the Euler-Lagrange equations in the context of graphs. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  This finding is further substantiated by the poor performance of an object detection system in a cluttered environment when it was assumed that all objects had unique poses.  This study provides insight into how recurrent neural networks facilitate efficient learning and categorization of complex visual data. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. Moreover, we observe that the topological characteristics of the extended Hatano-Nelson chain are analogous to those of a Sutherland lattice, which indicates the presence of topological correlations in the many-body system. The applications of topological quantum computing and artificial materials creation further emphasize the necessity of addressing correlation effects in systems with non-Hermitian topology. The study presented here provides a valuable contribution to this endeavor. \end{abstract}

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, but this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling blends with Coulomb interaction to alter material properties in a way that addresses the limitations of Pauling's second postulate.
Hydrogen's ability to form strong chemical bonds with silicon atoms makes it feasible to accurately control dopant positions, which can supplement silicon's inherent variability with quantum tunneling to surpass the limitations of Pauling's second postulate, thereby enabling the discovery of novel silicon-based quantum materials. 
In this review, we explore how paired hydrogen molecules in silicon defect lattices give rise to pressure and stress that adjusts the positions of near-by dopants by approximately 0.38 Angstrom, which can influence valence band near the Dirac point, adjust the bond lengths of adjacent silicon atoms, and generate pressure that changes the bond lengths of adjacent silicon atoms by approximately 10 Gigapascals.
Consequently, this arrangement of hydrogen molecules gives rise to pairs of dopants with unique and controllable electric properties called $\delta$-dopants, which can vary in position and cause local variations in the silicon crystal structure that can affect the positions of near-by dopants, which can influence valence band near the Dirac point.
This unique arrangement of hydrogen molecules in a silicon crystal not only expands our understanding of the structural dynamics of silicon-based electronic devices but also opens up new avenues for the discovery of novel silicon-based quantum materials and the design of multi-functional silicon devices that can harbor both quantum tunneling and Coulomb interaction. 
Ultimately, this combination of hydrogen molecules and dopants can give rise to unprecedented silicon materials that can inspire a new generation of silicon-based quantum computing technology.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world applications, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical implementations. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical applications of optimization techniques in solving complex problems. In conclusion, we emphasize the benefits of reproducibility in optimization research, discuss the potential future developments of our framework, and highlight its practical advantages over existing optimization software frameworks. Lastly, we outline the key considerations that should be taken into account in future-related hyperscale hypercomplex design projects. With its superior features and vast functionality, we believe LibOPT to be an indispensable tool for optimization specialists, as well as budding researchers entering this vibrant field of study. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the transfer of knowledge from jointly trained models, which has consistently delivered superior results in similar studies. Our models leveraged state-of-the-art Transformer architectures, trained on both enriched and standard datasets, to deliver outstanding outcomes. During evaluation, our models outshone other competitors by a significant margin, achieving remarkable accuracy and efficiency. Our analysis reveals that knowledge transfer played a key part in our success and provides valuable insights for developers to enhance misogyny identification models. Finally, our analysis highlights the limitations of current models and suggests possible improvements for the community to achieve total victory in this important challenge. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak network times by collecting and preprocessing data in advance. This method's main objective is to minimize average network strain while ensuring data accessibility when needed. This is achieved through cooperation among network participants. Extending this concept to a secure network requires an additional layer of security, introducing cryptography into caching and computation processes. A specific problem in this context involves a centralized entity called a Pioneer that distributes information in an encrypted and cached format to multiple users, while also maintaining access to the decryption key. This setting is known as the Private-Peering model and a relevant question in this context is how much network strain can be saved in this setting compared to a straightforward transmission method. This comparison is measured through metrics such as data transmission quantity and computation cost. This particular study focuses on data transmission quantity and, for a specific set of parameters, this study shows that the caching scheme with computed data in the Private-Peering model achieves the same level of security as previous schemes in the Public-Peering model but with a significant improvement in average network strain - an improvement of order O(N log N), where N represents the total number of users. Additionally, this study presents several enhanced methods that yield significant improvements over existing order O(N) methods, including one method that achieves a level of exponential improvement over existing methods when the network strain is high (up to O(2^(1-omega(N)/N)}) and another method that achieves a level of polynomial improvement over existing methods when the network strain is moderate (up to O(N^(1/(2 +/- epsilon)))). Further research in this area is presented in the thesis as problems to be addressed in the near future. This thesis also presents an alternative but related approach known as the Distributed Caching approach and provides a connection to a well-known caching problem known as the Sunrize problem. This approach focuses on saving network strain by efficiently distributing information to multiple users while ensuring data accessibility when needed. This is achieved through an entirely distributed mechanism and a related question in this context is how much network strain can be saved in this setting compared to a straightforward transmission method. This setting is known as the Sunrize model and, for a specific instance of parameters, this approach saves a factor of at least O(N) over existing methods when there is no prior knowledge of the target user. Additionally, this approach focuses on a related but more constrained problem known as the One-Time proposal problem and presents an efficient solution to this problem

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Instead, we utilize a specific form of inductive-inductive types that incorporate a "coinductive" aspect, which can be found in the Isabelle/ HOL-HOAS proof assistant and can also be used to define the lifting monad. We further observe that, in the context of univalent type theory, the lifting monad can be utilized as a fundamental concept to address partiality in mutually recursive data types, such as sets defined recursively together, which is an instance of mutually inductive definitions. We successfully define the Scott model for PCF with dependent pairs using the lifting monad, which serves as a model for weakly normalizing and terminating PCF with dependent pairs. Additionally, we establish that a normalizing model for PCF with dependent pairs is not possible if we require a predicative and constructive Scott model. We also address an alternative representation of partiality in univalent type theory based on universes, which allows for an alternative understanding of the Scott model for PCF, which uses a universe instead of the lifting monad. Notably, this representation of partiality has been used in other works, such as by Ahier et al. Based on our findings, we conclude that both the lifting monad and the universe provide suitable ways to handle non-terminating processes in univalent type theory. Finally, we outline future prospects for further research in this field. As an appendix to this work, we provide an extensive discussion of various alternative methods for understanding partiality in univalent type theory. This discussion aims to provide clarity on the specific approach used in this formalization and to summarize the different strategies for dealing with partiality in univalent type theory. Additionally, as an alternative, we also discuss a normalizing model for PCF with dependent pairs, which serves as an illustration of how different conceptual approaches to partiality can influence the understanding of normative and weakly normative domains

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Furthermore, the developed algorithm remains compatible with different types of geometric constraints. 
Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing safe navigation systems that take into consideration a robot's inherent geometry, especially relevant for robotic arms with spherical joints.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators - sentence overlap and edit distance - are employed for gauging sentence similarity. We investigate the impact of distinct graph constructions representing sentence meaning and their corresponding similarity metrics. A numerous dataset comprising diverse texts from multiple sources is utilized for demonstration purposes. Various graph-based methodologies, including the fundamental approach of matching sentences with highest similarity, are examined, along with more advanced strategies involving directed graphs, weighted indicators, and editorial distance analysis. Experimental outcomes indicate that the directed version of the shortest path algorithm outperforms other approaches, followed by the original shortest path algorithm, particularly when dealing with large datasets. Furthermore, we introduce a new technique called the hybrid strategy, directing the shortest path algorithm towards the optimal sentence with the highest similarity, which yields the best outcomes among all the examined strategies. Experimental results indicate a substantial improvement in accuracy using this hybrid approach. Lastly, we highlight the potential for applicability of the studied graph-based methods in numerous unrelated domains. This research is distinct from prior efforts in graph-based text summarization, presenting novel insights with significant implications. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we present a method to apply quantum interferometry and information processing effectively, based on a fully consistent description of BECs as classical nonlinear systems. This approach draws from existing solutions in classical nonlinear dynamics, and we demonstrate its feasibility through a simple example simulation. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to extend this method to quantum information systems, utilizing quasipatterns and other unique patterns that arise from solving nonlinear equations exactly. This enables the creation of reliable quantum gates, as well as precision measurements, in such systems.
