One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to the model's parameters. Our proposed algorithm was tested and demonstrated superior performance on three real-world datasets when compared to baseline methods. Our source code is available at https://github.com/jfgourdeau/DeepCoFi. Our results indicate that deep learning integration with collaborative filtering is an effective approach for building variability-optimized recommender systems. Our work aims to bridge the gap between theoretical and practical recommendations by addressing diversity as a critical aspect. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one random matrix perturbed by a free idempotent is a general phenomenon, accompanied by a continuum of phase transitions as the matrix's rank increases. This line of reasoning applies as well to the Berberian conjecture, addressing the freeness of Hilbert space projection lattices. Our methods draw from the mathematical analysis of complex systems, integrating results from statistical physics and the theory of freeness in operator algebras. Ultimately, we obtain empirical spectral distributions for various matrix perturbation problems that share a strong analogy with the Berberian conjecture. This line of reasoning applies as well to the perturbation of Gaussian and Berberian lattices. We observe a phase transition in the spectral distribution of a perturbed Berberian lattice for low-rank matrices,, accompanied by a phase transition in the spectral distribution of a perturbed Gaussian lattice for low-rank matrices,, known as the Nagao-Yamamoto phase transition,, which occurs for full-rank matrices under an infinitesimal perturbation,, known as the Zinn-James phase transition,, along with the detection of a phase transition in the spectral distribution of a perturbed Berberian lattice for low-rank matrices,, which converges towards the Nagao-Yamamoto phase transition for low-rank matrices under an infinitesimal perturbation,, with a phase transition in the spectral distribution of a perturbed Berberian lattice for low-rank matrices,, which converges towards the Zinn-James phase transition for full-rank matrices. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. Moreover, our approach applies equally to monitoring all of these models after reduction to Minimized B\"uchi Automata with No Epsilon Transitions. Empirical evidence underscores the practical efficacy of our proposed methods. Although online model checking is generally known for its worst-case linear complexity, our zone-based monitoring methods achieve average-case efficiency through a low quadratic complexity, making it suitable for practical use. Furthermore, our comparative experiments indicate that the symbolic online monitoring method outperforms the standard online model checking method, especially for large systems. The proposed techniques are made available as an open-source tool called Tegelaft. Tegelaft's main advantage lies in its ability to provide an earliest expected time for when a conclusive verdict can be given, in addition to the usual analysis it performs. As such, it can estimate the cost of monitoring real-time systems before actual knowledge of the system's execution timeline. We explore an approach to determine a dynamic cost adaptation method that helps adjust the monitoring effort according to the actual timing progress. In particular, the tool can provide an earliest expected time for deciding whether a system satisfies a given metric interval temporal specification when using a online method. When model checking is used, it can offer an earliest expected time for when a conclusive verdict can be given, updated periodically and fluctuating accordingly. For minimizing automata-based analysis, it can project the largest such automaton that accounts for possible timing errors, providing an earliest expected time for deciding system validity. In addition to these analyses, the tool can offer an earliest expected time for deciding whether a system accounts for all possible timing errors. The empirical evidence suggests that the zone-based method outperforms the standard model checking method, especially for large systems. As such, our comparative studies indicate that the average-cost efficiency of the zone-based method makes it practical for use. The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky characterization results having been documented. The results indicate that the camera meets the specified requirements of coordinate accuracy ($20 ~\mu\text m)$ and suffices for current science operations. The camera's performance meets scientific standards, but some minor adjustments are required to optimize its performance. The main limitation of the system lies in its thermal stability, as temperature fluctuations affect the camera's optical properties. The project has successfully demonstrated the capability of the camera, and plans are in place to upgrade the system in the near future to further enhance performance. The upgrade will utilize an advanced, more stable detector system to improve the camera's precision. The proposed modification includes the replacement of the current CCD detector with a CMOS detector, and subsequent redesign of the camera's optics to achieve enhanced field tracking capabilities. The proposed modification is anticipated to enhance the camera's precision by at least one order of magnitude, achieving the specified requirement of coordinate accuracy of less than $5 ~\mu\text m$. The upgrade will likely be completed by the end of 2017, with the modified camera set to enhance scientific observations in various fields, while facilitating the achievement of key scientific objectives of the GRAVITY project. The projected improvement in precision will significantly enhance the camera's ability to effectively utilize the VLTI's diverse configuration options, for science applications such as testing the divisibility of the ASPECS wavelength survey by the GRAVITY project, as well as probing the physics of gravity at unprecedented angles resolution. In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit state transition and is insulated from influence by the cavity by parity. By introducing an imaginary rotation of the qubit and cavity fields, we transform the Rabi model into a form that exhibits a protected emission of odd photons via a soliton-like solution, and this model can be realized with a QED system with a negatively charged impurity. The ultrastrong coupling regime enables the emergence of protected photon bundle emission as a robust quantum footer, facilitating the generation of multi-photon states and bi-photon entanglement. By adjusting the Rabi frequency, one can switch between photon bundle emission and conventional Rabi oscillations. The research paves the way for experimenting with protected photon bundle emission using state-of-the-art cavity QED technologies. Moreover, the approach can be extended to explore protected photon bundle emission in other quantum systems protected by parity symmetry. \textbf{Abstract published in Physical Review X 10, \textbf{040302} (2020)}.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. Additionally, the derived equation of state was used to determine the critical constants and other key properties of sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium, and francium. Furthermore, from this equation of state, mathematical formulas for speed of sound, thermal conductivity, and other property parameters have been obtained, thereby establishing a connection between these properties and the atomic properties of the alkali metals. It is anticipated that this equation of state will facilitate the evaluation of certain physical properties in high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. Lastly, the obtained results are deemed to be useful for creating predictive models of chemical and biological processes influenced by pressure. This proposed equation of state appears to be a versatile tool for addressing a diverse range of theoretical and practical issues. Lastly, potential future applications of this equation of state were considered, such as using it to determine the transport coefficients of alkali metal gases and assessing its validity against experimental data on potassium. 

For the purpose of this research, experimental data on the transport coefficients of alkali metal gases were graphically represented using mathematical formulas derived from the proposed equation of state, thereby illustrating their behavior under varying pressure and temperature conditions. It was observed that at lower temperatures and higher pressures, deviations from ideal behavior were noticed in the form of positive gas compressibility and negative thermal expansivity. These non-ideal tendencies in the transport coefficients were found to increase with increasing pressure and temperature. Furthermore, a comparison between the predicted and measured values of thermal conductivity revealed reasonable agreement, particularly at lower temperatures and higher pressures, thereby indicating that the proposed equation of state can accurately predict this property over a broad pressure range. Lastly, potential future applications of this research were considered, such as using it to determine the transport coefficients of alkali metal gases under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions and assessing its validity against experimental data on rubidium and cesium.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into the Caenorhabditis research code for performing simulations of scalar field perturbations and rotating black hole collapse. Our analysis shows that the residual errors in the Hamiltonian constraint are negligible compared to the numerical error, indicating that the solver converges rapidly. Additionally, we observe that the conformal structure of the initial conditions influences the solutions to the momentum constraints. This leads to certain degrees of freedom in the metric variables, which can be fixed by imposing appropriate boundary conditions or supplemental equations. Several strategies for addressing these issues are discussed, along with a variant of the method where the Hamiltonian constraint is satisfied by a conformally flat spacetime, removing the need for a conformal structure in the initial data. This approach is particularly beneficial for reducing the computational cost of solving the Hamiltonian constraint in simulations involving fundamental fields. However, it introduces pathological states, including spacetime singularities and nonphysical oscillations in the gravitational and field configurations, which must be removed through a nonlinear filtering process. This strategy is beneficial for reducing the degree of freedom in the metric variables, while ensuring that the residual errors in the Hamiltonian constraint do not impact the simulation results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the nonlinear filter does not alter the conserved quantities, while significantly decreasing the amplitude of the oscillations in the source terms. In practical scenarios like power consumption prediction and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy by around 10%. Notably, our model is also highly efficient, with computational complexity similar to the Transformer's linear scanning complexity. As such, we propose that the amalgamation of adaptive graph neural networks and the Transformer architecture represents a promising direction for the development of LSTF models. Our code is currently available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Chen-Ethan/MDCF_for_LSTF. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy by around 10%. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a circle from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a particular positive semi-definite matrix, which also determines the possible support of the Radon measure. The positive semi-definite matrix can be further interpreted as the Gramian matrix of an orthonormal basis for Kc and represents the maximum possible dimension of a finite orthogonal basis for the space of all low-frequency Fourier coefficients. The study also includes a stability analysis of BPC, which proves that the approximate solution with the minimum total variation among all compatible Radon measures is consistently convergent as the cutoff frequency approaches infinity. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. These tests confirm that the streamfunction-velocity formulation of the transport equation is resistant to numerical instability. In practical terms, this means that the first-order upwind stabilisation method serves as an effective stabilisation strategy for the transport of vector-valued fields. Furthermore, numerical results indicate that the mixed formulation of the transport equation is a suitable alternative to the enhanced formulation when the transported field is well approximated by a first-order function space. Nonetheless, the enhanced formulation remains the preferred choice when a high-degree approximation of the transported field is employed. Lastly, numerical results confirm that both proposed methods are capable of providing spatially high accuracy solutions for the vector transport equation. This research ultimately suggests that these methods can be adapted for use in the transport of vector-valued fields in rotating shallow-water models at the heart of global numerical weather and climate prediction models. In particular, these methods show particular promise for applications involving momentum transport and spiral gravity waves in two-dimensional models of the global tropics. In the future, the authors intend to adapt and implement these methods for use within three-dimensional global climate models, marking a key milestone towards enhancing the numerical solution of these models. In the longer term, the authors aspire to extend the methodology outlined in this research to accommodate the transport of additional vector-valued variables like elastic fields and wave solenoidal fields. By achieving this, the authors expect that the existing global numerical weather and climate prediction models can be revised to incorporate an advanced treatment of momentum and energy transport at their core, promising significant breakthroughs in modelling the coupled dynamics of global climate and wave phenomena. Overall, this thesis makes significant contributions to the fields of machine learning, computer science, and biomedical ethics. By employing a layer-wise approach to differential privacy, this research tackles the technical challenge of integrating privacy mechanisms with the training process of deep neural networks, a problem that has yet to be thoroughly addressed in the literature. From a practical standpoint, this research contributes to the development of end-to-end decision support systems, which maintain user data privacy and produce accurate, predictable results. By combining fairness and differential privacy, this research yields understandable predictions with quantifiable uncertainty, thereby navigating complex ethical considerations in deep learning technologies. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool powered by AI, which addresses the issue efficiently by converting a network into a node. This conversion enables NBcoded to operate on an FPGA, providing fast and accurate results in real-time, with the potential to expand into other applications. NBcoded's performance was evaluated on three different neural networks and showed promising results, with a 99% accuracy rate on specific data sets, along with a 75% reduction in resource requirements compared to existing solutions. The successful implementation of NBcoded opens up new possibilities for the development of software tools coded directly into an FPGA, enabling conversion of network elements into coded nodes and allowing multiple applications to share the same hardware resources. This enables innovative solutions for IoT and industrial healthcare systems, such as network traffic classification, malware detection, and performance monitoring, among others. In addition to its cybersecurity capabilities, NBcoded shows potential in optimizing computer vision applications on FPGA, offering a 2x speedup and reducing memory requirements by 5x. This research presents a groundbreaking innovation in coding and artificial intelligence, with a potential impact on various fields and applications. The innovative architecture of NBcoded, with its modular design, will likely drive future research and development in this area, paving the way for advanced microelectronics innovations. In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. 
Additionally, the hybrid method proved advantageous in resource allocation for non-convex optimization tasks. 
These findings support the potential of quantum computing, particularly hybrid approaches, as viable solutions for complex optimization problems in electrical engineering.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically establish physical laws based on measurement data, though this endeavor is plagued by inconsistencies. Current ML algorithms are plagued by issues of overfitting and non-fidelity to physical principles, hindering their effectiveness. A particular challenge arises in devising an efficient optimization strategy that balances data fit and adherence to physical principles. To address this, we propose an adaptive optimization framework, dubbed POD-GM-CCE, combining proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) with a Gaussian process (GP) model and constrained least squares optimization. This approach facilitates the effective separation of the physical mechanism governing the measured data and the noisy residual. By utilizing the constrained least squares method to resolve the multi-modal system, we ensure our results remain physically meaningful and scalable for handling complex real-world problems. We evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithm in two scenarios, namely, learning the Roelofs projective Schrödinger equation and the Navier-Stokes equations, with encouraging results. Our approach is characterized by its efficiency in capturing the underlying physical mechanism of the targeted problems. We successfully integrate our method with the residual optimization strategy, allowing the algorithm to refine its approximations by actively reducing excess model variability. This iterative technique enables continuous improvements, leading to ever-more accurate data fit without compromising its fidelity to physical principles. Moreover, our POD-GM-CCE method possesses inherent stability, due to the localized search, which enhances its overall robustness and performance. Overall, our research highlights the promise of our novel algorithm in automatically establishing universal physical laws from measurement data, while adhering to established physical principles. The detailed description of our algorithm is intended to motivate further research into the automatic construction of physical laws, potentially paving the way for revolutionary discoveries in multiple fields. To this end, we include an in-depth analysis of the computational costs associated with our approach, which is estimated to be in the order of $O(N \log^3N)$ per iteration. Notably, our proposed metric offers a more accurate reflection of the algorithmic complexity than the standard least squares method, which is characterized by a higher complexity of $O(N^3)$. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Notably, these decoders perform similarly to leading state-of-the-art traditional methods on average, while typically doing at least similarly in situations involving a single type of noise and often surpassing them in various other noise conditions. While the use of reinforcement learning leads to some increased overhead compared to traditional methods, the advantages in terms of computational expense make it a promising approach, especially considering potential applications in quantum circuits and resource estimation for fault-tolerant quantum computing. This research is expected to pave the way for the development of reliable quantum computers. These results imply that the removal of the medium effect allows for the identification of the response of the medium and the determination of the momentum of the hadron prior to interaction with the medium. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution scenarios. A major innovation of this work is the introduction of a model, named RICH-Net, which initializes networks using rich features in conjunction with an ensemble of regularizing mechanisms. Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including fluorescent properties. We've observed the formation of intricate 3D micro-endoscope illumination, miniature solar-powered water desiccation systems, and rapid localization of multiple spatial light points in both tissue types. These experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our integrated system over traditional GA-based systems. We've also calculated the energy efficiency of our wavefront manipulation system and found that it takes less energy to accomplish 3D tissue focusing compared to previous studies. This research represents a notable breakthrough over existing techniques in photon control technology and may open doors for the development of more efficient and cost-effective photoactivated chemical and biological treatments. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm called NV-RCABD is proposed to ensure system reliability by accounting for data fluctuations in system caches, with particular focus on detecting and recovering from crashes. This new algorithm is based on two key components: a checkpointer that periodically saves key information and a recovery process that compensates for any data losses resulting from crashes. A detailed analysis shows that NV-RCABD is both accurate and efficient, with performance that can be improved using various optimization strategies. This researcher further explores potential issues and introduces several variants of NV-RCABD to address these problems. Furthermore, a detailed examination is conducted to compare NV-RCABD with two existing algorithms: RV-RCABD and WRCABD. This comparison reveals that NV-RCABD outperforms RV-RCABD in terms of efficiency while introducing no new weaknesses, and also surpasses WRCABD in both efficiency and dependability. Details of each algorithm, along with their variants, can be found in the researcher's previous work [1]. Finally, a detailed examination is performed to demonstrate that NV-RCABD can be applied effectively in a non-volatile memory environment. This is achieved by converting the system into a synchronous system with the use of synchronization points, as data is flushed from the cache and into the main memory at these points. This conversion is confirmed to be precise and efficient, with details available in the researcher's previous work [2]. In conclusion, NV-RCABD is an advanced algorithm designed to ensure fault tolerance in high-performance computing systems, providing superior accuracy and efficiency. This researcher further presents various optimization strategies, a comparison with existing algorithms, and an application of NV-RCABD in a non-volatile memory environment. In addition, several variants of NV-RCABD are introduced to address potential issues, as detailed in the researcher's previous work [3]. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodicity across these systems: the escape probability distribution, the distribution of ergodic times, the scalar correlation function, and the escape time probability density for non-hierarchical systems. The findings showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, revealing a previously overlooked aspect: the influence of the angular distance between closest approaches in the escape probability. The distribution of ergodic times was found to be consistent across different scenarios, following a power-law pattern with a negative exponent. The scalar correlation function demonstrated time reversal symmetry, and within non-hierarchical systems, the distribution of ergodic times was uncoupled from the escape time probability density, displaying distinct scaling behaviors. The underlying mechanics of these statistical features can be interpreted through a unified theoretical framework, offering insights into the physical dynamics of these systems. The observed ergodic behavior in three-body systems sets the stage for exploring more complex astronomical phenomena, such as planetary scattering and close encounters, using a statistical approach. The research also paves the way for extending this methodology to study yet more intricate phenomena, like the dynamics of dust particles in plasma. The findings of this study are further expanded into an upcoming article, where we will delve into noise in three-body systems, including fluctuations in the angular distance between closest approaches and the statistical behavior of scattering angles. The upcoming article will particularly focus on the noise characteristics in hierarchical three-body systems, in addition to addressing whether these systems exhibit ergodic behavior when viewed from a celestial perspective. The noise analysis is particularly pronounced in systems where two bodies pass close to each other while a third observer is at a distant vantage point. The ensuing noise in the angular distance between closest approaches can be broken down into components stemming from the associated scattering angle and the distance between the observer and the two bodies that are interacting closely. The noise in the scattering angle, in turn, can be broken down into the noise in the distance between the two bodies and the noise in the approach distance, with the latter's contribution rising as the approach distance diminishes. The noise in the distance between the two bodies can be broken down into the noise in the exchange cross-section and the noise in the mass ratio, with the latter's contribution rising as the mass ratio decreases. This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we establish a representation of predicates from any given universe in continuous logic as subobjects in this category, resulting in a hyperdoctrine that is equivalent to the subobject hyperdoctrine. 
This allows us to leverage the existing theory of hyperdoctrines to study questions related to model theory. 
In particular, we define the notion of universal and existential resizing for continuous first-order logic models.

Finally, we show that a model possessing the existential resizing property also possesses the universal resizing property. 
This concludes that the existing valuation model for continuous first-order logic already demonstrates the existential resizing property.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis. This research showcases the efficacy of deep sequential models in forecasting complex mental health phenomena and highlights their potential for practical applications in real-world healthcare settings. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to utilize deep sequential models for the prediction of suicidal ideation. In addition, this research is in conformity with the guidelines set by the National Institute of Mental Health's Research Standards for Suicide Research, including informed consent requirements from participants. Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the viruses possess a specific structural component and are placed on surfaces with a specific type of carbohydrate layer. This raises hopes for the development of new treatment methods for influenza, as forcing the virus to stop moving could potentially freeze the viral movement machinery, making it immobile and thereby disabling its ability to spread. This could be achieved through an external force strong enough to overcome any resistance from the virus, as well as through the modification of surface carbohydrates to hinder the virus's ability to move. Furthermore, this study suggests that viral movement does not require specific viral proteins with inherent motility capabilities, as even randomly distributing the spike proteins on the virus can still activate this metabolic movement. Finally, this study reveals that viral movement may not be limited to carbohydrates on surface surfaces, but could also occur within the airways of hosts, as shown in recent findings. This changes the understanding of this phenomenon and its potential applications, as it could still be used to stop viral transmission even if the virus is internal rather than external. The potential implications of this research are vast and we hope they contribute to the development of new strategies for combating influenza. In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how nuclear displacement influences the electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to optics. However, connecting this effect to optics is possible through second-order spectroscopy, allowing the exploration of novel optical responses beyond linear phenomena. We demonstrate this connection by introducing new mechanisms for generating optical responses via second-order perturbation theory. These mechanisms include a beat charge mechanism, associated with changes in dielectric tensor elements, and a confluence mechanism, linked to the cross product of position operators. A specific example in $\beta$-beryllium aluminate, using both experimental and computational methods, reveals that the beat charge mechanism dominates its second-order electronic responses. Additionally, our findings suggest that beat charge mechanisms contribute substantially to all-electron second-order spectroscopy. This study lays a theoretical foundation for interpreting the observed electronic and phonon contributions in a previous study on $\beta$-beryllium aluminate. We also propose a practical approach for quantifying Born effective charges through experiments. We have developed a user-friendly code that integrates the proposed approach, allowing for its application in future research. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. The emergence of electrical currents within a topological insulator is investigated when it is exposed to external electromagnetic pulses, and the extent to which it is affected by the duration and intensity of these pulses has been quantified. The nonlinear magnetoelectric effect is found to be subject to an intrinsic bound known as the Landau-Penrose bound, and its predicted behavior holds true in various computational models. The nonsensical energy requirements of the Landau-Penrose bound can be satisfactorily resolved by replacing the protracted acceleration of the particle by rapid successive interactions that emit high-energy particles. The description of a topological insulator's response as an electromagnetic wave-like phenomenon whose direction of propagation is specified by an axially symmetric vector P, also known as the axion profile, offers a novel theoretical framework for the nonlinear magnetoelectric effect. The axion profile can be used to determine the energy requirements of the Landau-Penrose bound in terms of the particle's energy and the thickness of the topological insulator, providing a concrete estimate of this bound. The axion profile can be observed in various nonlinear magnetoelectric experiments, with the thickness of the topological insulator acting as the experimental variable to achieve this. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, stochastic lambda calculus denotational semantics is shown to naturally align with probabilistic recursion theory, a framework for constructive recursive probability theory. This connection relies on a core observation regarding the interaction between recursive and probabilistic structures. Finally, stochastic lambda calculus is shown to provide a suitable basis for developing a constructive version of Lebesgue integration integrated with recursive probability measures, thereby offering an alternative to Scott domains in the context of probabilistic domains. This research presents an innovative approach to developing an adequacy theorem for a higher-order probabilistic language. The presented work differs from earlier research on developing type-safe random number generators (Mellies and Tabaca, 2019) by incorporating random number generation as just one instance of a broader class of stochastic functions. The resulting theory is more general, encompassing random sampling as well as other conceptualizations of high-order stochastic operations, thereby offering greater flexibility in the design of stochastic type theories. The proof techniques employed in this research include novel constructions such as a stochastic bisimulation proof technique inspired by the fundamental back passage, as well as a constructive version of Tychonoff's theorem, tiling problems, and Tarski's greatest fixed point theorem. Specifically, this research develops an original and innovative solution to a tiling problem in the context of probabilistic domains by utilizing an iterative algorithm that generates a stochastic function that solves the problem. Similarly, this research develops an original and innovative solution to Tarski's greatest fixed point theorem in the context of probabilistic domains by utilizing an iterative algorithm that generates a stochastic function that solves the problem. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Nonetheless, further advancements in photonics and software analysis are required to fully leverage the benefits of this novel technique. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert behavior and simulator design, imitation performance deteriorates significantly.  To address this issue, we propose an iterative distillation method that leverages feedback from various sources, such as real-world experts, simulated analysts, and automated systems.  The model is trained by progressively condensing distributed knowledge into a singular, evolving policy.  Experimental evaluation conducted across diverse domains confirms that our approach outperforms existing imitation learning techniques by roughly doubling success rates in challenging situations.  Moreover, we successfully apply this method to control tasks, such as autonomous driving, and simulate analyst feedback using generative models to simulate human behavior. Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time. A comprehensive set of simulations demonstrates that the proposed method effectively converges to an accurate map and Situational Awareness is achieved quickly, with performance comparable to an ideal scenario where the map is known beforehand. Additionally, a practical implementation of the method as a UAV mission is showcased, highlighting its potential in various applications. A relevant discussion on potential challenges and aspects of the method is included in the companion technical report. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. These findings are expanded to include the logistic and normal models with mixing distributions and ARD models. Finally, the relationship between GMLE and the minimum variance unbiased estimator is analyzed. All the results are accompanied by solved exercises. This research is an extension of previous work on estimating a parameter matrix based on its expected value under independent row distribution (Cheng, Li and Zhang, 2019). This research has been extended to apply to both row and column distributed idempotent and non-negative semi-idempotent matrices. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon a unified model for combining independence and interdependence of data records. This paper quantitatively examines the trade-offs between data utility and privacy for various data distributions, such as Bernoulli and Poisson models. By developing accurate bounds for different privacy parameters, the researchers validate the efficiency of OSDP in boosting data utility by distinguishing between sensitive and non-sensitive data records. Moreover, the findings provide practical guidance to data collectors on setting appropriate privacy parameters based on their data's statistical properties. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of OSDP in boosting data utility while safeguarding privacy. The research showcases OSDP's suitability for applications like building automation systems, customer behavior analysis, and electronic commerce transactions. A practical implementation of OSDP can be accessed through an open-source C++ library available at https://osdp.github.io/. The purpose of this paper is to pave the way for future research in this field; consequently, all relevant code and data have been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/osdpresearch/OSDPtradeoffs. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
We observed that CO column density could be linked to surface-density fluctuations or chemical alterations, while C$_2$H column density was tied to changes in the C/O ratio rather than surface density changes in the gas.
However, our models require the presence of a massive planet (with a mass greater than 0.2 times Jupiter's mass) to explain this degree of gas depression.
But such a finding conflicts with the constraints set by the dust emission patterns and the gas pressure profile as measured through gas kinematics.
Our modeling suggests that a reduction in local CO abundance is essential in explaining the observed CO structure and that this factor outweighs any potential effect of a planet on the gas surface density. 
This study forms part of a special issue on the Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series focusing on the MAPS program. 
For more information on this research, see arXiv:2104.12799 and the associated special issue for AS 209: arXiv:2104.12800, as well as the associated publication for CT Chamaeleon: arXiv:2105.04325. 
Our team also explores the physics behind the gas substructures in protoplanetary disks using comprehensive modeling in another research paper.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency. This paper introduces ETA's fundamental concepts, showcases its capabilities, and highlights its innovative features. Furthermore, we compare ETA's performance with other time-stamped data analysis tools, demonstrating its exceptional speed and adaptability. Lastly, we outline exciting perspectives for ETA's future development. ETA is freely accessible at https://eta.hepann.org for Linux and Windows platforms. This website serves as the primary hub forETA's documentation, as well as its package updates. ETA's source code is also available at https://eta-hepann.org/source for users who wish to contribute or run ETA on a single board computer. ETA supports the acquisition of time-stamped data from various detectors via an API that is similar to ParaMonte's monte-carlo simulation interface, as well as its various analysis tools. This uniform approach facilitates the seamless integration of ETA with ParaMonte, enabling users to generate synthetic event data to analyze alongside experimental data. This collaboration has resulted in an integrated software framework referred to as peta. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are incapable of retaining internal momentum, nor do they exhibit expected signs of gravitational binding. Instead, these structures appear to be dispersing throughout the galaxy, with no evidence of shared origin based on their membership, and movement patterns, further indicating that they are merely coincidental groups of stars within the galaxy. We propose the term "stellar string" as an appropriate descriptor for these structures, encompassing all known examples, and suggesting they might be an indication of the resolved structure of larger stellar components, such as the Gaia-Enceladus structure. We also discovered multiple structures, yet unclassified, exhibiting similar characteristics, and suggest that they might be an indication of the varied, distinct origins of the galaxy's stellar components. We constructed a model illustrating the predicted movement patterns of these structures, comparing the results to observed data, and finding some correspondence. In the course of our research, we developed an efficient technique for identifying and mapping these structures, utilized in all our analyses, and made available for future research. In conclusion, our research successfully employed Gaia data to map the galaxy's stellar structure, demonstrating the utility of Gaia data in this endeavor, and showing the need for precise 3D mapping, and extensive analysis, incorporating diverse stellar properties, to gain a deeper comprehension of the galaxy's composition and structure. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must manually assemble full outfits. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Visual Incompatibility Metric (VIM), enabling us to measure the degree of visual incompatibility in outfits rather than simply classifying them as fully compatible or not. VIM is based on three key visual attributes - top and bottom style similarity, color harmony, and type consistency - enabling it to accurately predict visual incompatibility even in outfits with small mismatched items. To showcase its effectiveness, we implemented VIM using SqueezeNet and tested it on the Fashionista dataset, demonstrating its capability to pinpoint individual garments contributing to an outfit's overall visual incompatibility score. This enabled us to enhance an existing Outfit Maker app with an interactive compatibility slider, allowing users to adjust the strictness of the app's compatibility criteria and easily try on more fashionably compatible outfits. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This research demonstrates that in a system that looks static on a large scale, local patterns of failure can develop differently based on small-scale dynamics. Moreover, our findings highlight the importance of considering all relevant time scales when analyzing a system. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our study on the strain-mobility trends discloses a nonlinear correlation. Moreover, our model suggests that matching GaN to an imaginary solid solution composed of Zn$_{0.75}$Ge$_{0.75}$Mg$_{0.25}$Si$_{0.25}$N$_2$ could increase its hole mobility by 160%. These computations provide theoretical groundwork for developing GaN materials with elevated hole mobility. Moreover, the used numerical methods can be extended to design other nitride semiconductor materials with optimized electron or hole effective masses. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region. Additionally, we discuss specific cases of surfaces that satisfy the $L$-condition and explore some remarkable examples. These examples include a one-parameter family of surfaces that have a Hopf differential similar to that of a flat surface, as well as a set of surfaces that have a Hopf differential similar to that of a Gaussian sphere. We also show that these examples fit within a broader category of surfaces called pseudoholomorphic surfaces. These examples provide valuable insight into the geometry of isothermic surfaces with unique Hopf differentials. Conversely, we use these examples to construct pseudoholomorphic surfaces using the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Finally, we explore the relationship between these examples and a one-parameter family of surfaces that have a Hopf differential similar to that of a compact surface with a unique geometric property. We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in approximating $P$ when the underlying probability measure has singular boundaries. To achieve this approximation, we utilize a novel method of decomposing Hilbert-Schmidt operators into a sum of a conditional mean operator and a conditional mean-zero operator, which has potential applications in various fields. A numerical study confirms the efficacy of this approach in practicing least squares linear regression with noisy observations. This paper complements a prior study by provides a more precise approximation of $P$ when the underlying probability measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Moreover, the approximation methods proposed in this paper can be adapted for solving integral equations with non-smooth kernels despite similar challenges. Our work is self-contained and does not rely on the prior study or other research in this field. Furthermore, one of the main tools used to achieve this approximation is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H_K$. By assuming the reproducing property of $P$ within this space, we can approximate any operator that shares this property, which has potential applications in various domains, such as the approximation of conditional expectation, functional linear regression, and time series analysis. In practice, this reproducing property facilitates the efficient computation of $Pf$ using the kernel trick for certain kernels, which simplifies the regression task. To overcome the potential issue of overfitting, we employ regularization techniques in reproducing kernel Hilbert space regression and establish the rate of convergence for the estimated operator, which achieves optimal performance when the true conditional expectation operator is Hilbert-Schmidt. This research is further enhanced by a prior study but offers a more precise approximation of the conditional expectation operator when the underlying probability measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, with most studies focusing on developing novel embedding techniques, but providing little to no consideration for temporal factors. In contrast, this paper proposes a straightforward yet effective method to incorporate temporal information into knowledge graph embeddings, which shows significant improvements over traditional models in testing experiments. The proposed solution has two key components: first, temporal information is represented as an extension of existing graphs, rather than a rival to be incorporated through a soft alignment process, and second, a straightforward regularization approach that minimizes discrepancies between embedded and actual temporal relationships. The proposed solution demonstrates the highest performance in testing experiments when compared to traditional graph embedding techniques. The source code of this study is available at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/TemporalKGE for the sake of reproducibility. The code can be used by other researchers to verify the results of this study or apply the proposed method in different scenarios. We establish that two graph C*-algebras are Morita equivalent if their graph currents under strong shift equivalence relations are also Morita equivalent, thereby providing a characterization of strong shift equivalence through Morita equivalence. This characterization holds for arbitrary graphs, and it aligns with a prior finding by Raeburn and Sault, although our examination is distinct as it involves first-order principles. Additionally, it allows us to demonstrate that the graph C*-algebras constructed by Pask, Raeburn, and Sault are Morita equivalent, as well as those constructed by Clark and Farthing. Furthermore, this characterization leads to a new interpretation of their work, and it paves the way for a simplified proof of a prior open problem by Hirch, Ortega, and Pask, Raeburn, and Sault. In addition, it allows us to extend the findings to continued fraction algebras and inverse semigroups as well as determine that the first-order principles do not automatically extend to second-order principles. Lastly, it leads to a new characterization of first-order strong shift equivalence relations, thereby providing an alternative to a characterization given by Hirch, Ortega, and Pask, Raeburn, and Sault. In the process, it examines and compares the relationships between strong shift equivalence, Morita equivalence, and Fell bundles as well as their connections to ideal-related and unitary equivalent relations. This investigation culminates in the formulation of two open problems. \par The investigation is organized into seven sections, with an appendix containing additional material. It is an adaptation of the author's doctoral dissertation at the University of Nevada, Reno. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density oscillations and the atmospheric background temperature, specifically at temperatures above 150~K. Conversely, this association disappears at temperatures below 150~K. This distinct behavior is attributed to the interaction between GWs and the atmospheric CO$_{2}$ frozen into the soil, which begins to vaporize at temperatures above 150~K. This new understanding has significant implications for the interpretation of GW data obtained from previous and current missions, spanning the martian sky. Additionally, the observational evidence obtained from the MAVON instrument suggests that the atmospheric flow induced by GWs is not confined to the lower martian atmosphere but rather extends all the way to an altitude of approximately 120~km. This is supported by a comparison with atmospheric models, which often underestimate the intensity and vertical distribution of GW-induced density oscillations in the upper martian atmosphere. Lastly, the observational data appears to rule out a previously proposed hypothesis suggesting that the interaction between GWs and the martian atmosphere leads to a vertical exchange of momentum that is restricted to a layer above an altitude of approximately 100~km. Instead, the data suggest that the same process is characterized by a more straightforward vertical decay with altitude. This is, however, an observational conclusion that is subject to modification based on new model predictions. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilizes a novel spectrogram-based quality measure. These spectral samples are transformed into waveforms using a window-based generator, which significantly enhances the generation speed. Since there are limited tools for automatically assessing the quality of synthesized soundscapes, we introduce FID and MKL, a family of metrics relying on Melception, a novel audio classification model designed to evaluate the authenticity and relevance of synthesized soundscapes. Our model exceeds the performance of the VQGAN baseline according to FID, yields relevant results on MKL, and produces high-fidelity sounds with clear, crisp dynamics. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software. A particular focus will be on the LSTM and LSTM-like variants, as well as less commonly exploited recurrent models, including the MRNN and the MIMO MCT network. We will also examine specialized training methods for object tracking, including gradient-assisted optimization, latent model learning, generative model tracking, deep learning for multiple object tracking, and our latest contributions to the field. This comprehensive article is intended to provide a thorough understanding of recurrent neural networks, their variations, and cutting-edge techniques for tracking multiple objects. This research was motivated by our previous studies on object tracking, a task that requires combining top-down information with bottom-up cues within a sequential process. This is particularly interesting from a biological perspective, as it shares similarities with the human visual cortex, a key area of study in computer vision. Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel model type, referred to as SO-SIR models, capturing the effects of pandemic control interventions on the economy, is developed in conjunction with the aforementioned inequality, which indicates the required severity of restrictions in relation to the timing of the response. Through numerical simulations of the model, aligned with real-world pandemic and economic patterns as observed in the EU, US, and China, the benefits of an optimal two-stage strategy become evident, which exemplifies the 'economic irreversibility' concept in action. Furthermore, the model offers policy advice by predicting the ideal moment to initiate a stricter measures regime, which corresponds to the point at which the pandemic's economic impact begins to accumulate irreversibly. On a broader scale, the model provides a means for evaluating the global pandemic management policies required to mitigate the resulting economic consequences. A key outcome reveals that a universal, effective, and equitable pandemic management strategy under the guidance of 'economic irreversibility' could potentially generate significant economic rewards for all participating nations, which in turn, could lead to increased cooperation in the face of a global health crisis.
